Don't forget the CX! How Clay puts agents out onto Slack for support but still rates the 'human in the loop' Bookmark icon Read later Summary: Humans with experience in support are still performing best, but agentic tech is finding its role in Clay's customer help operation.











A question that enterprises are staring to ask themselves as the agentic revolution rumbles on is whether the Customer Experience (CX) is going to be the same if users are talking to a human or an AI. The answer may be somewhat nuanced. Clay is a US AI firm set up in 2017 with a mission today to, in its own words, “power GTM (go-to-market) engineers: Our goal is to give every company the tools to build their own revenue system, guided by the belief that we started with: give creative people powerful building blocks and let them shape those blocks around their ideas”. Customers include the likes of OpenAI, Stripe, HubSpot, Uber, Box, and Mistral. The firm also has a claim to fame as the first firm to use Fin’s AI agent technology to scale customer support inside its Slack community. According to George Dilthey, Clay’s Head of Support: Clay's support has always been centered around Slack. Our Slack community was was really one of the earlier big growth moments that we had. Even as we've rolled out some more traditional channels, like the in-app messenger or email or whatever it might be, Slack has always still been a centerpiece for it. This Slack centricity is different due to the public domain nature of the community: It's out there in the public, and so the risk is a little bit higher. The way that you think about it is, ‘OK, can we do this? My CEO is looking at these Slacks, and our co-founders, everybody's there. Other customers are looking at it, so if there are policies that apply differently to different customers, you have to think through those things. So, just being out in public is just a little bit changes the game a little bit. The other thing is that the expectation of privacy is just very different. We have a lot of things that we're starting to build out with Fin, where it has access to your billing information or your table data or whatever it might be in the app, and we can't just throw that stuff out into a public forum. So we actually, in a lot of ways, have to have a de-graded experience for Fin on Slack, not because the capability is not there, but because we have to think about that sort of that that rollout a little bit differently. CX to the fore Keeping Customer Experience (CX) front-and-center here is a strategic priority for everything to do with AI rollout, adds Dilthey: Our Head of CX always talks about no matter what you're doing with these AI things, you always want to think about the Customer Experience first. Being in Slack means that we can meet our customers where they're at, and and having that experience, not only in our community, but also with our enterprise customers and their Slack channels, just makes it really nice, meeting them where they're working and be able to keep that seamless. In terms of its overall use of Fin’s agents, Clay has done a lot to build out its capabilities, with a focus on two things in particular - the context that Fin has and the data that Fin has. In the context portion, Dilthey elaborates: We're thinking about this knowledge base, which used to be this place that would get updated once every three months - maybe. It was always out of date and didn't update with the same cadence as the product was shipping. We've had to re-think the way that we think about that context. Can we make it self-healing? Can we use cloud-managed agents that run over our knowledge base on a regular basis to make sure that we're we're keeping up with releases and changes in the product. So, we're thinking a lot about context. Also front of mind is the role of data connectors and what access Fin has, Dilthey adds: What we sort of started to realize is that the kind of work that we're doing with Fin is actually the same work that we'd want to do for any agent. I was starting to see other parts of the company doing very similar things with our Sales Enablement docs internally. How do we think about keeping that content up-to-date, and how do we think about keeping our engineering on-boarding up-to-date or whatever it might be? It really applies anywhere, even more on a macro-level. How do you know that what is in Slack is up to date? All of that becomes so much more important in this agentic era because you have to you have to really be specific about the things that it is pulling from. That’s led to what Dilthey alludes to as “some really interesting moments”, explaining: I'm getting pulled into conversations to think about these problems in other parts of business, even in the way that we're building our product, we're building agents in our product. I'm learning from that, and talking to the engineers that are building that out, because a lot of it is just a lot of the same process. It's been really fun to see where that can apply differently. It's sort of like, you know, ‘The tide rises all boats’ kind of thing. Great expectations It’s not only the tide rising though; so too is the floor of what is expected from support. Dilthey says: Where we used to have regular product support specialists and then enterprise product support specialists, we've flattened that a little bit, because all of the questions that are making it to humans are the harder ones and the enterprise ones, and we have to be a little bit more strategic and think about those a little bit more, a little bit differently. But now that our humans are focused on that, we want to start thinking about the ‘human in the loop’ opportunity. I used to think of AI support as very much like either AI handles it or a human handles it, and now I think there's a really interesting middle ground where I can speed up my team, when they're checking logs or they're checking whatever it might be, whether it's through Copilot or a ‘human in the loop’, just make those processes that they're doing faster at that kind of stuff. Getting more human? And he’s conscious that agents capabilities are evolving all the time: The more exposure they can get to these things, with the judgment they have, the knowledge they have, they can pro-actively identify things that, in theory, a human could if they had all the time in the world, but in practice, they can't. That’s good though, yes? Up to a point, it seems: It's scary too because you want to give [agents] access to to everything to be more effective, but you also have to be careful about the things that you're throwing out there. And there is still much to be said for human experience coming into play, he notes: I find that the folks that are still the best in our team are the ones that were good five years ago, before there was AI. We're starting to shift the types of questions that they're answering, that human aspect and that strategic thinking and that that pattern matching, across different things that you're seeing in the queue. How they collaborate internally with Product and Engineering, all of that becomes so much more important and is so much more frequent, because you're not just answering the password reset questions anymore. There's a level of curiosity and adaptability that [humans] have, that they've had since before the AI world. Being able to carry that through, even as they make themselves faster using AI, has been really kind of fun to see.

proofCandidates.title: Clay’s Kareem Amin joins Disrupt 2026
proofCandidates.summary: Clay co-founder and CEO Kareem Amin will present at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 on how AI created the GTM engineer role. Clay tripled annual recurring revenue to $100 million and raised a $115 million Series D at a $7.1 billion valuation. The session explores AI-native go-to-market systems.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Two years ago, most companies didn’t have a GTM engineer. Now the role is showing up across tech, with practitioners using AI and automation to build revenue systems that once required multiple people, tools, and manual processes.

What changed — and what does it mean for the way companies find customers and grow?

At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, Clay co-founder and CEO Kareem Amin will take the AI Stage for “The GTM Engineer: How AI Created Tech’s Next Big Job Category.” He’ll trace how AI has changed the traditional go-to-market stack and helped create a new discipline in its place, giving attendees a look at what AI-native GTM looks like in practice and how it’s changing company growth.

Image Credits:TechCrunch

AI is giving go-to-market teams new ways to research prospects, work with data, personalize outreach, and automate workflows that once moved between separate tools and teams. As those capabilities converge, companies are rethinking not only their GTM technology, but also who builds and manages the systems behind growth.

If you’re building a company or rethinking how your team approaches sales, marketing, and growth, this is a new role worth understanding. Secure your Disrupt pass and see where GTM engineering fits into the next generation of go-to-market. Get a second pass at a 50% discount, and more savings for groups of four or more.

What does a GTM engineer actually do?

Traditional go-to-market work can involve hours of researching accounts, cleaning data, qualifying leads, preparing outreach, and moving information between systems. GTM engineering uses AI, data, and automation to turn more of that work into repeatable systems.

Clay coined the role in 2023. Its own GTM engineering guide describes GTM engineers as practitioners who build automated revenue workflows rather than executing individual GTM tasks by hand. The company says roughly 100 GTM engineering job listings are now appearing each month, including roles at companies such as Cursor, Lovable, and Webflow.

At Disrupt, Amin will put the shift into context and explore what AI-native GTM looks like in practice. Get your ticket to Disrupt to understand a role that barely existed a few years ago but could change how your next sales, marketing, or growth team operates.

Clay puts AI to work across the GTM stack

Clay started in Brooklyn in 2017 with one goal: Give more people access to the power of programming. Its original spreadsheet let users connect information and automate work without writing code. When salespeople, growth teams, and agencies began using it to find and reach customers, Clay followed them into go-to-market.

Today, the company provides infrastructure for GTM teams to access data, run agentic workflows, and launch campaigns. Its OpenAI-powered agent, Claygent, automates research and outreach for sales, marketing, and recruiting teams.

That evolution has been accompanied by rapid growth. TechCrunch reported in February that the company had tripled annual recurring revenue to $100 million in a year and announced an employee tender offer at a $5 billion valuation. Clay has continued growing since then, announcing a $115 million Series D in September at a $7.1 billion valuation.

Clay is also investing directly in the job category at the center of Amin’s Disrupt session, announcing a $1 million scholarship fund in September to train GTM engineers.

For companies trying to determine where AI can make a meaningful difference in revenue operations, add Amin’s session to your Disrupt agenda and see how one company is putting that model into practice.

From product leader to a new GTM approach

Kareem Amin co-founded Clay in 2017 and serves as its co-founder and CEO. Before Clay, he was VP of product at The Wall Street Journal and co-founded collaboration startup Frame, which Sailthru acquired in 2012.

Amin started Clay around the idea of putting programming capabilities into more people’s hands. AI eventually gave that idea a new application: enabling GTM teams to build systems that automate research, data enrichment, and outreach without relying on traditional engineering resources for every workflow.

Want to understand what a GTM engineer could mean for your own growth strategy? Secure your Disrupt pass and hear directly from one of the founders helping define the category.

See what AI-native GTM looks like in practice at Disrupt

GTM engineering may be a new job category, but the problem it addresses isn’t: How do you find and reach the right customers without simply adding more people and more tools? At Disrupt, you can see how AI is changing that equation — and meet the people building what comes next.

“The GTM Engineer: How AI Created Tech’s Next Big Job Category” is one of 200+ sessions across six industry stages, roundtables, and breakouts at Disrupt, taking place October 13-15 at Moscone West in San Francisco. More than 10,000 founders, investors, operators, and tech leaders are expected, along with 250+ speakers and 300+ exhibiting startups.

In addition, matchmaking, dealmaking, and networking give attendees opportunities to meet potential customers, investors, partners, and other founders confronting many of the same growth challenges.

proofCandidates.title: Government Buying Signals and Public-Records Procurement Data Are Now Available in Clay
proofCandidates.summary: Pursuit announced its public-sector data, including verified contacts, entity profiles, and buying signals, is now available in Clay. The integration covers over 170,000 public sector entities, with more than 160 million government documents analyzed in the past six months. The data is accessible through Clay's native enrichment step.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Government Buying Signals and Public-Records Procurement Data Are Now Available in Clay

Pursuit Logo The Clay x Pursuit Integration brings verified SLED contacts, entity data, buying signals, and FOIA-sourced intelligence into Clay as a native enrichment step ANN ARBOR, MI, UNITED STATES, September 30, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Pursuit, the revenue intelligence platform for teams selling into state, local, and education (SLED) markets, today announced that its public sector data is available in Clay. Clay customers can now enrich accounts and contacts with verified government contact data, structured entity profiles, live buying signals, and procurement intelligence sourced from public-records requests, without leaving their Clay workspaces. Clay gives go-to-market teams one place to source and enrich their data. SLED is where that gets harder to do, because a county government, a school district, or a special district isn't described by the firmographics and corporate email patterns that commercial data is organized around. Teams with a public sector motion have typically worked those accounts by hand, outside the workflows they run everywhere else. The Clay x Pursuit Integration brings that segment into the same system. Government entities, the people inside them, and the purchasing activity that signals an opening are now available in Clay as a native enrichment step, sourced from the primary documents agencies publish and the records they release on request. A team can build a SLED territory list, enrich it with verified contacts, layer on live buying signals, and route the result to a sequencer or CRM in the same table where it runs the rest of its pipeline. Four Pursuit capabilities are available in Clay: Find Your TAM sources public sector accounts as net-new rows by state, entity type, and budget range, covering cities, counties, school districts, and special districts.

Enrich Contacts returns verified titles, emails, and bounce risk mapped across the buying committee, including planning, IT, finance, and leadership roles.

Buying Signals adds live buying indicators to an existing account list, including budget approvals, contract expirations, leadership changes, and new initiatives, sourced from meeting agendas and department plans. "Public sector data doesn't behave like commercial data. There's no standard schema, no central registry, and most of what matters is a PDF on an agency website or a record you have to request," said Brandon Max, CTO and Co-founder of Pursuit. "We've spent years turning that into something structured and queryable. Putting it behind Clay's endpoints means a team can use it the way they use every other data source, instead of treating government as a separate project." Pursuit monitors more than 170,000 public sector entities and runs an industrial-scale public-records operation to obtain the contracts and purchase orders that name an agency's current vendor, what it pays, and when the agreement expires. Over 160 million pages of government documents have been analyzed in the last six months alone. That material is not published anywhere and does not exist in commercial data sets. It is now retrievable in Clay. Pursuit's Contacts, Entity, and Signals data is available in Clay now. FOIA-sourced procurement data is arranged through a Clay account team. About Pursuit Pursuit is a revenue intelligence platform for the state, local, and education market. Pursuit reads millions of government documents each month across more than 170,000 public sector entities and operates an industrial-scale public-records program to surface incumbents, pricing, and renewal timing. Every signal arrives scored against a customer's ideal customer profile with a verified contact attached. Learn more at pursuit.us. About Clay Clay is the infrastructure that go-to-market teams use to build their revenue system. It unifies all of a company's customer and market data with third party data from 200+ data vendors, lets you orchestrate any sales or marketing play, and deploys GTM agents that research, prioritize, and take action. Clay customers can execute any creative GTM idea to grow their company to its full potential.

proofCandidates.title: Landbase Launches GTM-3 Omni: New Benchmark Shows AI Agents Beat Clay, Apollo and ZoomInfo on List Precision
proofCandidates.summary: Landbase launched GTM-3 Omni, an AI agent for go-to-market discovery, and published benchmark results. The model achieved 76.7% list precision, outperforming Clay (47.9%), Apollo (36.0%), and ZoomInfo (23.2%) across 26 prompts. Landbase claims this precision can double campaign performance.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Landbase Launches GTM-3 Omni: New Benchmark Shows AI Agents Beat Clay, Apollo and ZoomInfo on List Precision
Instead of reps filtering and burning credits, one prompt does the targeting, qualification, enrichment and scoring. Customers see 2x the connects and meetings.
SAN FRANCISCO, September 29, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Landbase, the GTM infrastructure company for the agentic era, today announced the launch of GTM-3 Omni, its next-generation model for agentic go-to-market discovery, qualification and outreach, and published the benchmark results behind it.
Where GTM-2 unified natural language targeting with omnichannel campaign strategy, GTM-3 answers a harder question: can an agent reason over business data better than a human working a filter-and-keyword tool? Landbase's AI Lab built a benchmark to settle it.
Four vendors (Landbase, Clay, Apollo and ZoomInfo) were each given the same 26 list-building prompts, the same qualification criteria and the same judge. Every company and person each vendor returned was independently re-verified and scored against identical standards. The only variable was what each vendor returned.
| Vendor | Precision | Most precise list (of 26 prompts) |
| Landbase (GTM-3 Omni) | 76.7% | 18 |
| Clay | 47.9% | 4 |
| Apollo | 36.0% | 1 |
| ZoomInfo | 23.2% | 0 |
Landbase achieved 76.7% precision, compared with 47.9% for Clay, 36.0% for Apollo and 23.2% for ZoomInfo. Landbase won 18 of 26 prompts outright and delivered the highest first-page accept rate: 76.1% of the first 100 rows a buyer would actually work.
"Landbase was founded on the premise that you should no longer work for your software; your software should work for you," said Daniel Saks, Co-Founder and CEO of Landbase. "We've now proven that AI can automate the work, from TAM mapping to list building to account research, so reps can do more of what they love: selling and cultivating human relationships."
Precision Over Speed, by Design
GTM-3 Omni is not the fastest way to produce a list. A filter-based tool returns rows in seconds. GTM-3 takes roughly two minutes, because it plans the search, qualifies every candidate against the buyer's actual criteria and discards what doesn't hold up.
That trade is the product. A rep working a 77%-precise list of 1,000 companies has 767 real conversations available. The same rep on a 36%-precise list burns two out of every three touches on the wrong account and pays for the volume. Landbase customers have observed 2x or better campaign performance once list precision improves.
"With Landbase, agents can explore and reason over data to optimize go-to-market workflows with greater efficacy than humans. Landbase outperforms alternatives at identifying desired prospects by 2x in precision. When paired with targeted outreach, more precise audiences can drive 2x or greater improvement in campaign performance."

proofCandidates.title: How debate over an invoice prompted this AI startup to reimagine its coaching program
proofCandidates.summary: Clay, an AI sales startup, is expanding its coaching program after a debate over an invoice. Headcount grew from 80 to 600, and the company closed an $115 million funding round. It will pilot targeted coaching for first-time managers, with performance metrics to evaluate outcomes.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Total Rewards How debate over an invoice prompted this AI startup to reimagine its coaching program Moments of rapid growth are a good opportunity to remake the case for certain employee benefits, Clay’s head of people said.

Clay, an AI sales and marketing startup, is scaling rapidly. The company’s headcount went from 80 to 600 employees over the last year, according to its head of people, Alex Shapiro. And it recently closed an $115 million funding round, a development that’s likely to add more fuel to Clay’s growth. Moments like this are a good opportunity to remake the case for certain employee benefits, Shapiro said, and Clay’s longtime coaching program is one offering that recently warranted a second look. Shapiro recently told us how the benefit is evolving, thanks in part to input from Clay’s head of finance, Karan Parekh. Coaching at Clay. The startup, which was first founded in 2017, has long offered professional development coaches to any employees interested in these services. Clay built the program in-house, hiring a roster of coaches who could bill the company up to $5,000 a month, or the equivalent of 10 sessions, Shapiro said. Shapiro said the coaching program is a hallmark of the company’s “individualistic” culture, as leaders seek to support employees on their own personal journeys and career paths. At the time Clay’s founders developed it, they were interested in shepherding employees through “moments of change and growth when we don’t have a structured people team.” This goal continues to be relevant today, during “a moment of extreme growth” for the company, Parekh said. “We’re asking a lot of our employees, and so there’s an obvious value to being able to give them the scaffolding and resourcing that they need to navigate that change.” Turn and face the (Clay) changes. As Clay evolves, it stands to reason that its coaching program should evolve. Shapiro recently made the case to expand Clay’s roster of coaches, as well as bring on coaches who are more suited to targeted interventions with specific types of employees. A more targeted coaching approach might involve bringing on someone to work specifically with first-time managers of managers, for example. “That was a place where I thought, really specifically, we might want to look from an organizational structure standpoint. Somebody who’d never had direct reports before who now was managing several layers,” she said. The catch? Offering more bespoke coaching services would likely mean making a deeper investment in the coaching program. An invoice for one of these targeted coaching services prompted Shapiro and Parekh to engage in a debate about whether such coaches were worth the investment. Keeping track of benefits spending can be particularly challenging for a high-growth company like Clay, where headcount shifts so often, Shapiro said. Moments like this debate prompt her to ask herself, “did I actually just add a bunch of money on top of an already large line item, or did I think full stack about that entire investment in that bucket?” Beyond input→output. Clay’s people and finance chiefs ultimately came to a consensus by aligning themselves on the goals of the coaching program, Parekh said. They decided to pilot a program offering more targeted coaching interventions, with the goal of offering better support to first-time managers. It’s unclear which approach will yield better outcomes for the company, but Parekh said he’ll be looking at metrics like performance by teams with managers who are taking advantage of the new coaching offerings. Given the pace of change at Clay right now, Parekh said he feels comfortable being “a little bit more generous, forward leaning, and experimental in some of these programs.” During his back-and-forth with Shapiro, he said he’d learned that “it’s okay if something doesn’t have a direct input-output,” even if that’s the type of benefit he’s most comfortable with as a finance chief. Measuring return-on-investment doesn’t have to be all about numbers, he suggested. “We can kind of observe the things qualitatively that suggest that we should try something here and see what happens, and I think that’s okay, too.”

proofCandidates.title: Du CRM aux “buying signals” : la nouvelle bataille de la SalesTech
proofCandidates.summary: SalesTech is shifting from CRM to buying signals, using public data like job postings and funding rounds to detect purchase intent. Companies such as Clay, Apollo.io, and Common Room are building platforms that score organizations' readiness to buy. The competitive focus moves from contact databases to signal freshness and contextualization.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Du CRM aux “buying signals” : la nouvelle bataille de la SalesTech
📩 Pour nous contacter: redaction@frenchweb.fr
Pendant plus de vingt ans, les logiciels commerciaux ont été conçus autour d’une logique simple : centraliser des contacts, suivre des opportunités et organiser les pipelines de vente. Le CRM est devenu l’infrastructure dominante des équipes commerciales modernes, structurant aussi bien la prospection que le pilotage du revenu. Mais cette architecture montre désormais ses limites.
L’explosion des outils d’automatisation, des plateformes d’enrichissement de données et des modèles génératifs a profondément modifié l’économie de la prospection B2B. Trouver des contacts n’est plus un avantage compétitif. Générer des séquences d’emails non plus. Les outils capables de produire des centaines de messages personnalisés en quelques minutes ont abaissé le coût marginal de l’outbound à un niveau inédit. Résultat : les boîtes mail des décideurs sont saturées.
Dans ce contexte, la question centrale n’est plus seulement “qui contacter”, mais “pourquoi maintenant”.
Une entreprise qui recrute un directeur cybersécurité, qui ouvre un bureau en Allemagne, qui publie une offre d’emploi liée à l’IA générative ou qui annonce une migration cloud expose involontairement des signaux opérationnels. Ces événements deviennent des indicateurs d’intention d’achat potentielle. C’est précisément sur cette couche que se repositionne une nouvelle génération d’acteurs de la SalesTech.
Des sociétés comme Clay, Apollo.io ou Common Room développent des architectures capables d’agréger des données publiques, comportementales et contextuelles afin d’identifier les moments où une organisation entre dans une phase de transformation susceptible de déclencher une décision d’achat.
Le marché évolue ainsi d’une logique de gestion de base de données vers une logique d’intelligence contextuelle.
Cette transition modifie profondément le rôle du CRM historique. Pendant longtemps, des plateformes comme Salesforce ou HubSpot ont constitué la source principale de vérité commerciale. Désormais, la valeur se déplace vers des couches périphériques capables de capter des signaux extérieurs à l’entreprise : recrutements, mouvements de dirigeants, lancements produits, évolution réglementaire, publications financières, activité sociale ou participation à des événements sectoriels.
Le CRM conserve son rôle transactionnel. Mais l’intelligence commerciale migre progressivement vers des moteurs de détection d’intention.
Cette évolution reflète également une transformation plus large du fonctionnement des organisations commerciales. Les équipes SDR ont longtemps été pilotées sur des métriques de volume : nombre d’emails envoyés, appels réalisés, séquences déclenchées. L’IA remet en cause cette logique. Lorsqu’un agent peut générer automatiquement des milliers de messages personnalisés, la différenciation ne réside plus dans la capacité d’exécution, mais dans la qualité du ciblage.
Le signal devient plus important que le volume.
Cette dynamique favorise l’émergence d’une nouvelle catégorie de données : les “buying signals”. Derrière ce terme se cache une tentative de modélisation probabiliste du comportement d’achat des entreprises. L’objectif n’est plus simplement d’identifier une société appartenant à un segment pertinent, mais de détecter le moment précis où une contrainte interne, une transformation organisationnelle ou un projet technologique augmente la probabilité de conversion.
Certaines plateformes analysent ainsi :
- les créations de postes,
- les changements de stack technologique,
- les levées de fonds,
- les expansions géographiques,
- les publications GitHub,
- les annonces presse,
- les échanges communautaires,
- ou encore les comportements de navigation.
Ces données sont ensuite traitées via des modèles de machine learning et de NLP afin d’attribuer des scores d’intention ou des probabilités d’engagement.
Cette approche rapproche progressivement la SalesTech des logiques historiquement utilisées dans le renseignement économique et l’OSINT. Les plateformes commerciales deviennent des moteurs de corrélation de signaux faibles. Leur objectif n’est plus uniquement d’automatiser une séquence commerciale, mais d’anticiper des dynamiques organisationnelles avant qu’elles ne deviennent visibles dans le pipeline.
Dans cet environnement, la bataille concurrentielle change de nature. Pendant des années, les acteurs de la SalesTech se sont différenciés sur la taille des bases de données de contacts. Désormais, l’enjeu porte sur :
- la fraîcheur des signaux,
- la capacité de contextualisation,
- la pertinence des corrélations,
- la vitesse de détection,
- et la qualité des modèles d’interprétation.
La donnée de contact devient une commodité. Le contexte devient l’actif stratégique.
Cette mutation pourrait également redistribuer la chaîne de valeur logicielle du marché commercial. Une partie des plateformes historiques risque d’être reléguée à un rôle d’infrastructure transactionnelle, tandis que la valeur analytique se déplace vers des couches IA spécialisées capables d’orchestrer le ciblage, la priorisation et l’exécution commerciale.
À terme, la frontière entre CRM, veille stratégique et agents IA commerciaux pourrait disparaître. Les futures plateformes ne se contenteront probablement plus de suivre les opportunités déclarées par les équipes commerciales. Elles chercheront à détecter automatiquement les transformations internes des entreprises avant même que les besoins ne soient explicitement formulés.
Dans la SalesTech, l’enjeu n’est plus uniquement de gérer des relations commerciales, mais de modéliser le moment où une organisation est prête à acheter.

proofCandidates.title: AI Agents Are Replacing Human Workflows — What Founders Need to Know in 2026
proofCandidates.summary: Four AI agent startups raised $2.77 billion in September 2026, with Cognition leading at $2 billion for its Devin software engineer. The funds target eight workflows including legal, sales, and financial operations, with Harvey, Clay, and Ramp also raising. Founders are advised to price per outcome and build human escalation mechanisms.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Four companies announced rounds within 48 hours in September 2026 that tell you exactly where the next $10 trillion of startup value is being created. Harvey raised $550 million to build AI agents that execute legal work autonomously. Clay raised $115 million to build AI agents that run sales workflows end-to-end. Cognition raised $2 billion at $48 billion valuation to build Devin — an AI agent that writes, tests, and deploys software. Ramp is targeting $60 billion building AI that automates corporate financial operations. The pattern is identical. AI agents. Not AI tools. Not AI assistants. Autonomous AI systems that execute professional work from start to finish. Follow AI startup news at Startup Pill.
What Is an AI Agent and Why It Changes Everything
An AI tool assists a human with one step — generate a draft, answer a question, summarise a document. An AI agent executes an entire workflow autonomously — research a lead, draft personalised outreach, send the email, track the response, update the CRM, schedule the follow-up. The agent replaces a workflow. The tool accelerates a step. The commercial difference is enormous. A tool reduces one person’s time on one task. An agent eliminates the need for a human on an entire category of work.
Agentic AI is the term investors and founders use to describe AI systems with the ability to take autonomous actions, use external tools, browse the internet, write and execute code, and complete multi-step tasks without human guidance at each step. Cognition’s Devin is an agentic AI — it does not just suggest code. It writes, tests, debugs, and deploys it. Read AI startup strategy at Startup Pill.
The 8 Human Workflows AI Agents Are Replacing in 2026
Software development — Cognition’s Devin raised $2 billion at $48 billion valuation building an AI software engineer that writes, tests, and deploys production code autonomously.
Legal research and drafting — Harvey raised $550 million. 80 percent of Am Law 100 firms use AI agents for contract review, due diligence, and litigation support.
Sales prospecting and outreach — Clay raised $115 million at $7.1 billion. Its AI agents research prospects, personalise messages, and run outreach sequences without human input per contact.
Financial operations — Ramp is targeting $60 billion for AI that automates expense management, accounts payable, procurement, and corporate card operations.
Compliance monitoring — AI agents that continuously monitor regulatory changes, flag compliance risks, and generate audit-ready documentation are replacing quarterly human compliance reviews.
Customer support — AI agents that handle tier-1 and tier-2 support tickets end-to-end — reading, researching, responding, escalating — with no human in the loop unless the agent flags a case it cannot resolve.
Data research and analysis — AI agents that gather data from multiple sources, clean it, analyse it, and produce reports that previously required teams of analysts are deployed across finance, consulting, and market research.
Content and marketing operations — AI agents that research topics, draft content, optimise for SEO, and publish across channels are replacing large content and marketing teams in fast-moving organisations. Also read why vertical AI beats generic AI in 2026 and how startups go from zero to IPO. Follow AI agent startup news at Startup Pill.
How to Build an AI Agent Startup. The Founder Playbook.
Identify the workflow, not the industry. The best AI agent opportunities are not defined by industry. They are defined by workflow characteristics. The ideal target workflow for an AI agent is repetitive, high-volume, based on consistent input types, produces a predictable output format, and currently requires significant professional time to complete. Billing reconciliation, contract review, lead research, insurance claim processing, and clinical documentation all share these characteristics.
Measure output quality before pitching. AI agents live or die on output reliability. An AI sales agent that writes 70 percent of outreach emails well enough to send unsupervised is commercially valuable. One that writes 50 percent well enough creates more human review work than it saves. Define your quality threshold before your first customer conversation and show them the data.
Price per outcome, not per seat. AI agents replace workflows. Price accordingly. A legal AI agent that completes a contract review in 10 minutes instead of 4 hours is worth pricing at a percentage of the time saved, not at a monthly software subscription per user. Outcome-based pricing aligns your revenue with the value delivered and creates an economic argument that seats-based SaaS cannot match.
Build the human-in-the-loop escape valve. Enterprise buyers will not deploy fully autonomous AI agents in high-stakes workflows without a reliable mechanism to flag cases for human review. Build the escalation path first. Buyers who trust your escalation mechanism will extend agent autonomy gradually. Buyers who discover errors without an escalation path will remove the agent entirely.
Key Takeaways
AI agents replace workflows while AI tools accelerate steps. Four companies raised $2.77 billion combined in September 2026 building AI agents for legal, sales, software development, and financial operations. The 8 workflows AI agents are replacing in 2026 are software development, legal research, sales prospecting, financial operations, compliance monitoring, customer support, data research, and content operations. The AI agent founder playbook is workflow identification, output quality measurement before pitching, outcome-based pricing, and a human-in-the-loop escalation mechanism.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is an AI agent?
An AI agent is an autonomous AI system that executes multi-step tasks end-to-end without requiring human input at each step. Unlike AI tools that assist with individual actions, AI agents complete entire workflows — researching, drafting, sending, tracking, and updating systems — autonomously.
What is the difference between AI tools and AI agents?
AI tools help humans complete individual steps faster. AI agents replace the human across an entire workflow. A sales AI tool drafts one email when prompted. A sales AI agent researches the lead, writes a personalised sequence, sends it, tracks opens, and schedules a follow-up — all without being prompted after the workflow begins.
Which AI agent startups raised the most money in 2026?
Cognition raised $2 billion at $48 billion for its Devin AI software engineer. Harvey raised $550 million for legal AI agents serving 80 percent of Am Law 100 firms. Clay raised $115 million at $7.1 billion for sales AI agents. Ramp is targeting $60 billion for financial AI automation.
How do I build an AI agent startup?
Pick a workflow that is repetitive, high-volume, uses consistent input types, and produces a predictable output. Measure output quality against a professional standard before your first customer conversation. Price per outcome rather than per seat. Build a human escalation mechanism that enterprise buyers can trust before deploying full autonomy.

proofCandidates.title: Clay Closes $115M Series D, Doubling Valuation to $7.1B Amid Demand for AI-Griven Go-to-Market Tools
proofCandidates.summary: Clay raised $115 million in a Series D round, valuing the AI go-to-market software company at $7.1 billion. The company has over 17,000 customers, including 80% of Forbes AI 50, and has raised $392 million total. It also announced a $1 million scholarship fund for GTM engineers.
proofCandidates.fullText: Clay, the New York-based artificial intelligence go-to-market software company, said on Sept. 9 that it raised $115 million in a Series D round that valued the business at $7.1 billion, more than twice the $3.1 billion mark it reached in a CapitalG-led financing in August 2025. Wellington Management led the latest round, with backing from Sequoia, StepStone, Andreessen Horowitz, Perennial, Meritech, DST, CapitalG and other investors. Clay was founded in 2017 by the trio of former Microsoft engineer Kareem Amin, developer and designer Nicolae Rusan, and Varun Anand, a former political aide to the Hillary Clinton campaign in 2016. The company says its technology helps marketers identify the “next best action” for a business and then helps teams execute it. Just as software engineers run coding agents, so-called GTM Engineers run growth agents, Clay said. “AI is unleashing the biggest wave of company creation in history, and Clay’s goal is to be the engine those companies use to grow to their full potential,” said Amin, who previously served as product vice president for The Wall Street Journal. “We started by aggregating the best data for B2B companies. Then we built the infrastructure to run any personalized campaign on top of it. Now we’re building agents that can help grow your company for you.” The company said it now has more than 17,000 customers, including about 80% of the Forbes AI 50, and counts Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, Stripe, ElevenLabs, Workday, Siemens, Visa and UPS among its users. Clay describes its platform as a set of agents and workflows that connect CRM data, product usage information and outside signals to run personalized sales and marketing campaigns. The new financing underscores continued investor appetite for AI applications aimed at revenue teams, especially software that automates prospecting and outreach. Reuters reported the same valuation and round structure, while BetaKit also matched the $115 million Series D and roughly $7 billion valuation, reinforcing the scale of the deal. “We’re building a self-learning revenue engine,” Amin said. “The better a company gets at learning, the faster it grows.” Clay also said it was creating a $1 million scholarship fund to train what it called “GTM engineers,” a role it is helping define as AI tools reshape sales operations. On its funding page, the company said it had raised $392 million in total as of June 30 and pointed to fourfold revenue growth in 2025, though it did not disclose additional financial details in the latest announcement. [Noah Wire Services helped in the writing of this article.]

proofCandidates.title: Clay Raises $115 Million at a $7.1 Billion Valuation
proofCandidates.summary: Clay raised $115 million in a Series D round led by Wellington Management, valuing the AI sales software at $7.1 billion. The company's annual recurring revenue surpassed $100 million in December 2025, with revenue expected to reach $200 million this quarter and nearly $240 million by year-end. Management expects revenue to double next year.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Clay, a company specializing in AI-powered sales and marketing software, has raised its valuation to approximately $7.1 billion after closing a $115 million Series D funding round led by Wellington Management, more than doubling its previous $3.1 billion valuation in 2025.

The round included investors such as Sequoia, Andreessen Horowitz, Perennial, Meritech, DST Global, CapitalG, BoxGroup, Boldstart, Bloomberg Beta and Evolution.

The funding comes several months after a secondary share sale by the company’s employees in January 2026, which valued Clay at approximately $5 billion.

From $1 Million to $200 Million in Revenue

Clay’s growth has extended beyond its rising valuation. Its annual recurring revenue (ARR) surged from around $1 million to $100 million in just two years, with the company surpassing the $100 million mark in December 2025.

Annual revenue is expected to reach approximately $200 million in the current quarter and nearly $240 million by the end of the fiscal year, following roughly fourfold revenue growth in 2025.

The company’s management expects revenue to double again next year, driven by an expanding customer base and greater adoption of AI tools to automate sales and growth operations.

How Clay Evolved from a Software Tool into a Sales Platform

Clay was founded in New York in 2017 by Egyptian entrepreneur Kareem Amin and Nicolae Rusan, initially with the aim of making programming more accessible to non-specialists.

However, growing adoption of the platform by sales and growth teams gradually pushed the company to shift its focus toward software for Go-to-Market teams. The platform combines company data, research and automation tools, and AI applications to support lead discovery and outreach.

Varun Anand joined the company in 2021 and became a co-founder, while Rusan later left the company.

Companies including Anthropic use the platform for prospecting, while Airbnb relies on it to identify potential hosts for its Experiences service. DoorDash uses Clay to identify companies that could be targeted for its employee meal program.

Valuation Surpasses $7 Billion

The new funding marks a significant increase in Clay’s value from approximately $1.25 billion at the beginning of 2025, before rising to $3.1 billion in its previous funding round and then $5 billion in the January 2026 employee share sale.

Despite this growth, the company currently has no plans to go public, according to Kareem Amin.

Clay is now looking to expand the use of AI agents to automate more sales and growth-related tasks, while continuing to grow its customer base and platform-generated revenue.

proofCandidates.title: Clay Raises $115M Series D
proofCandidates.summary: Clay, a New York-based AI go-to-market company, raised $115 million in a Series D round at a $7.1 billion valuation. The round was led by Wellington, with participation from Sequoia, a16z, and others. The company will use the funds to expand its AI growth engine and support a $1 million scholarship fund.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Clay Raises $115M Series D at $7.1B Valuation

Clay, a New York-based AI go-to-market company, has raised $115 million in a Series D funding round at a $7.1 billion valuation. The company provides a platform that helps businesses identify ideal customers, monitor intent signals, and automate growth strategies through AI agents.

Investors

The round was led by Wellington, with participation from Sequoia, StepStone, Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) Perennial, Meritech, DST, CapitalG, BoxGroup, Boldstart, Bloomberg Beta, and Evolution.

Clay Use of Funds

The company plans to use the capital to further its mission of building an AI-powered growth engine and to support its newly announced $1 million scholarship fund, which is designed to train the next generation of go-to-market engineers.

About Clay

Founded in 2017 by Kareem Amin and Nicolae Rusan, with Varun Anand joining as a co-founder in 2021, Clay provides an AI-driven system that unifies internal business data with external signals to help teams execute growth workflows and build autonomous revenue systems. Headquartered in New York, the platform is currently used by over 17,000 customers.

proofCandidates.summary: Clay raised $115 million in a Series D round led by Wellington Management, valuing the company at $7.1 billion. proofCandidates.fullText:
Clay Raises $115 Million To Build AI Sales Teams for B2B Sales Growth

By Ekemini 11 September 2026

Key Takeaways Clay secured $115 million in Series D funding, boosting its valuation to $7.1 billion.

The platform combines internal data and external market signals to power automated AI growth agents.

Clay created a $1 million scholarship fund to train future GTM engineers and growth leaders.

Finding customers takes forever. Sales teams spend most of their day chasing leads and writing emails one by one. As AI gets better, companies want to know if they can also have an AI sales team. For this reason, Clay raises $115 million to build software that can sell for businesses. Clay Hits $7.1 Billion After $115M Raise New York-based startup Clay announced it raised $115 million in a Series D round. The round was led by Wellington Management. Other investors include Sequoia, Andreessen Horowitz, StepStone, Perennial, CapitalG, and more. The startup is currently valued at $7.1 billion. That’s more than double. Last August 2025, Clay was worth $3.1 billion after raising $100 million. More Updates: Kinetix AI Raises $75M To Scale AI Data Model Hardware How Clay Creates AI Agents That Sell For You Clay started in 2017 as a tool to pull together B2B company data. Then it built software to run personalized marketing campaigns. Now it’s building AI agents that actually grow your company for you. Clay looks at your customer list, how people use your product, emails, calls, and even news like who got funding or who’s hiring. Then the AI decides who to talk to, what to say, and when to say it. It can find the right customers, spot when they’re interested, tell the right people about new features, and send the emails for you. CEO Kareem Amin calls this a self-learning revenue engine. The more it runs, the more it learns about your business and customers, and the better it gets. Clay also coined the term “GTM Engineers.” GTM means Go-To-Market. Just like software engineers run coding agents, GTM engineers run growth agents. Clay Pushes for More Revenue and Training Clay’s revenue is growing fast. CEO Amin said annualized revenue this quarter will hit about $200 million, up sharply from last year. Co-founder Varun Anand forecasts $240 million by year end, and double that next year. The company says it kept costs low and was even profitable for a short time this year. With the new money, Clay will keep building agents and expanding. It also announced a $1 million scholarship fund to train more GTM Engineers. Clay will also preview new products at its user conference “Sculpt” on October 8 in San Francisco. More Updates: Boring Company Raises $3B for Dubai Loop Network AI Is Moving From Writing to Doing Investors are pouring money into AI agents that don’t just draft an email but actually do the job. Wellington’s tech investing head, Rob Masone, believes that the opportunity Clay has is huge. Masone believes that it is becoming increasingly clear that the startup goes beyond the category of existing sales tools. AI is moving from being a copilot to being the driver. Instead of helping a sales rep write, Clay runs the whole growth workflow. Anthropic uses Clay to automatically research sales targets. Airbnb uses it to find hosts for its Experiences business. DoorDash uses it to find companies for its employee lunch program. The Bigger Picture: AI for Business Growth The Clay AI fundraising shows where VCs think AI is headed next. Founder Kareem Amin put it simply: AI is unleashing the biggest wave of company creation in history, and Clay’s goal is to be the engine those companies use to grow to their full potential. Founded in 2017, Clay spent 6 years searching for product-market fit before landing on sales teams. Now it’s hitting $100M+ ARR and growing fast. More Updates: Positron AI Raises $875M to Scale AI Inference Hardware

proofCandidates.title: Clay lands $115-million USD Series D at $7-billion valuation
proofCandidates.summary: Clay, a Canadian-founded go-to-market startup, closed a $115-million Series D round at a $7.1-billion valuation. The round, led by Wellington, values the company more than double its prior $3.1-billion valuation. Clay has surpassed 17,000 clients, including Anthropic, ElevenLabs, Google, OpenAI, Siemens, and Stripe.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Canadian-founded go-to-market startup wants to become “the AI growth engine for every company.”

Canadian-founded, New York City-based go-to-market (GTM) startup Clay has closed another major financing, securing a $115-million USD ($159 million CAD) Series D round.

The news: Clay develops and sells AI software and agents designed to help other firms automate marketing, sales, and other GTM tasks. The company announced its Series D on Wednesday. It was led by Wellington, with support from Andreessen Horowitz, CapitalG, Meritech, Sequoia, and others. The round values Clay at $7.1 billion USD, more than double the $3.1-billion USD valuation it was given with its $100-million Series C in August 2025. It comes as Clay surpasses 17,000 clients, up from 10,000 a year ago, including Anthropic, ElevenLabs, Google, OpenAI, Siemens, and Stripe.

From the source: “AI is unleashing the biggest wave of company creation in history, and Clay’s goal is to be the engine those companies use to grow to their full potential,” Clay co-founder and CEO Kareem Amin said in a release. “We started by aggregating the best data for [business-to-business] companies. Then, we built the infrastructure to run any personalized campaign on top of it. Now, we’re building agents that can help grow your company for you.”

The context: Clay was launched in 2017 by McGill University graduates and repeat entrepreneurs Amin and Nicolae Rusan. Rusan (who is Canadian) has since left Clay. Amin, who is originally from Egypt, attended McGill before moving to the United States over a decade ago. There, he built a New York startup with Rusan called Frame, an e-commerce tech firm they sold to Sailthru in 2012. Clay, which also counts Canadian-founded Maple VC among its early investors, was recently featured on VC Antoine Nivard’s Dominion List, which tracks influential Canadian founders building in the US.

Final thought: Clay has invested heavily in developing “a self-learning revenue engine” featuring agents capable of autonomously finding prospective clients, monitoring their intent, drafting personalized outreach, and updating customer relationship management systems. “Just as [large language models] predict the next best word in a sentence, Clay will predict the next best action to grow your business,” Maple VC general partner Andre Charoo told BetaKit. Charoo added that he thinks Clay has the potential to become the agentic successor to Salesforce.

Feature image courtesy Clay.

proofCandidates.title: Venture Capital & Startup Funding Roundup, September 9, 2026: Coatue, Andreessen Horowitz, Greylock, Kleiner Perkins, Sequoia & More
proofCandidates.summary: Ten venture rounds totaling roughly $1.47 billion were reported on September 9, 2026, with about 91% concentrated in six deals. The largest was Harvey's $550 million at a $15.5 billion valuation, while others included Cylake, Solstice Oncology, and Clay. Capital is shifting toward companies that control high-value workflows like legal, sales, and weather operations.
proofCandidates.fullText:
0 Shares

Venture capital’s center of gravity today isn’t in one neat category called AI. It is moving toward companies that control high-value workflows: legal work, sales, wealth management, cybersecurity, industrial production and even weather-risk operations. The ten most consequential rounds verified inside the past twelve hours total roughly $1.47 billion, with about 91% of that capital concentrated in the six largest financings. That distribution is telling: investors are still willing to write very large checks, but mostly where they see a path to owning an operational system rather than selling a thin feature on top of somebody else’s model. The biggest signal came late in the research window. Legal AI company Harvey announced a fresh $550 million round at a $15.5 billion valuation, while Lightfield surfaced with a $47 million Andreessen Horowitz-led Series A aimed directly at rebuilding customer relationship management for an agent-driven software era. Between those two poles sit a $245 million cybersecurity financing for Cylake, an unusually large $225 million Series A for Solstice Oncology, and triple-digit rounds for Clay, Perry Weather and Savvy Wealth. The Macro Environment: Capital Is Moving From Models to Operational Control The venture market is drawing an increasingly sharp distinction between companies that merely use artificial intelligence and those that can turn it into a durable system of record, execution or infrastructure. Harvey is becoming an operating layer for legal work; Clay and Lightfield are competing to control customer data and revenue workflows; Euno wants to supply the organizational context that autonomous agents need; CloudNC brings AI into CNC machining. These are not ten variations of a chatbot. They are attempts to insert software into processes where errors are expensive, data accumulates over time, and switching costs can become substantial. That helps explain the check sizes. Investors appear increasingly comfortable funding AI applications at infrastructure-like valuations when those applications sit directly in the flow of work. Harvey has gone from an $8 billion valuation in December 2025 to $11 billion in March and now $15.5 billion in September. Clay, meanwhile, has more than doubled its valuation from $3.1 billion in August 2025 to $7.1 billion today. The market is effectively saying that a small number of application companies may become very large platforms if they own proprietary workflow data, distribution, and execution rather than relying solely on model differentiation. The public-market backdrop is supportive but not indiscriminate. Barclays raised its 2026 S&P 500 target on strong corporate earnings and continued AI spending, while simultaneously warning about demanding valuations, persistent inflation, geopolitical risk and a more hawkish rate environment. That combination helps explain why private capital is concentrating rather than spreading evenly: when the cost of being wrong remains high, investors gravitate toward category leaders, clear enterprise budgets, technically differentiated security products and software connected to measurable operating outcomes. Secondly, a less visible thread running through today’s deals: the digitization of physical and regulated operations. Perry Weather sells safety and weather-operations software; WINT addresses water management; CloudNC automates precision machining; Solstice is applying venture-scale capital to immunotherapy development. Capital is not abandoning software. It is expanding software’s addressable territory into sectors where operational data, regulation, physical assets, or scientific risk create stronger barriers to entry than a generic AI interface can provide. Top Funding Rounds Harvey raises $550 million to turn legal AI into an enterprise operating layer Harvey is the day’s largest qualifying round and arguably its clearest valuation signal. The San Francisco legal AI startup raised $550 million at a $15.5 billion valuation, with new investors Diffusion and Lightspeed Venture Partners co-leading. Existing investors, including Sequoia, Kleiner Perkins, Andreessen Horowitz, Coatue, Conviction, GIC, and Goldman Sachs Alternatives, also participated. Harvey builds AI software for law firms and corporate legal departments, covering contract analysis, due diligence, compliance, and litigation workflows. Why does a vertical-software company need this much capital? Harvey increasingly behaves less like conventional SaaS and more like an applied AI platform. The company says it will put the financing into model training, product expansion and international hiring, and it also announced the acquisition of agent-security startup Guardrails AI — Harvey’s fourth acquisition this year. Its valuation has risen from $11 billion in March to $15.5 billion now, a roughly 41% step-up in less than six months. Reuters reported in March that Harvey had already raised more than $1 billion; adding today’s round takes disclosed cumulative funding above $1.55 billion. The competitive implication extends well beyond legal tech. Harvey demonstrates that application-layer companies can command model-company-style financing when investors believe the application owns valuable data, domain-specific evaluation, customer relationships and the workflow itself. The risk is equally clear: at $15.5 billion, Harvey must grow into a much larger revenue base while competing with specialist rivals such as Legora and Clio, as well as broader AI platforms entering professional services. Reuters noted that Harvey is already used by 80% of the 100 highest-grossing U.S. law firms, giving investors evidence that distribution is becoming a genuine barrier rather than a theoretical one. Funding Details

Startup: Harvey

Investors: Diffusion, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Sequoia, Kleiner Perkins, Andreessen Horowitz, Coatue, Conviction, Elad Gil, Evantic, GIC, Goldman Sachs Alternatives, Verified Capital, WNDR, Sapphire Ventures, Whale Rock

Amount Raised: $550 million

Total Raised: More than $1.55 billion based on disclosed funding

Funding Stage: Growth financing; round label not disclosed

Funding Date: September 9, 2026

Headquarters: San Francisco, California

Sector: Legal AI / Enterprise Software Cylake raises $245 million to build a cybersecurity platform for operational sovereignty Cylake raised $245 million in convertible notes from Lightspeed Venture Partners, Picture Capital and Redpoint Ventures. Axios describes the Sunnyvale company as building a cybersecurity platform for “operational sovereignty,” while the funding announcement says Cylake is approaching the beta release of its next-generation security product. The most interesting part of the deal is not simply its size but its structure. A $245 million convertible-note financing ahead of broad product disclosure gives investors exposure while postponing the valuation mechanics that normally accompany a priced venture round. That is unusually substantial optionality capital for a cybersecurity company at this point in its public life. It suggests Lightspeed, Picture and Redpoint see a potential platform opportunity large enough to justify funding ahead of clearer commercial benchmarks. A broader security thesis is embedded here. As companies deploy autonomous software into production, cybersecurity increasingly has to protect not just networks and identities, but an organization’s ability to keep operating when software, agents, credentials, or infrastructure are compromised. Cylake has not yet disclosed enough publicly to judge how differentiated its architecture will be, so view the financing primarily as a strong investor signal rather than proof of product-market leadership. The large convertible structure also makes valuation conclusions premature. Funding Details

Startup: Cylake

Investors: Lightspeed Venture Partners, Picture Capital, Redpoint Ventures

Amount Raised: $245 million

Total Raised: Not disclosed

Funding Stage: Convertible-note financing

Funding Date: September 9, 2026

Headquarters: Sunnyvale, California

Sector: Cybersecurity / Operational Resilience Solstice Oncology launches with $225 million in funding to advance next-generation cancer immunotherapy Solstice Oncology launched with a $225 million Series A led by RA Capital Management, joined by Canaan Partners and Forbion. The Boston biotech is focused on a second-generation CTLA-4 immunotherapy program and is associated with Harbour BioMed, which announced the financing for its partner company. A $225 million Series A is notable even by biotech standards. It shows that while general venture markets are concentrating around AI, specialist life-sciences funds remain willing to assemble very large syndicates at company formation when the therapeutic thesis and development path justify it. RA Capital, Canaan and Forbion are not funding a broad software-style experimentation cycle; they are funding clinical development where capital requirements arrive early, and failure can be binary. Strategically, Solstice also illustrates why biotechnology has not been displaced by the AI funding boom. Software can often reach market with progressively larger rounds. Drug companies may need hundreds of millions before commercial validation because clinical programs, manufacturing, regulatory work, and trials are expensive. Investors therefore care less about early revenue and more about the quality of the biological hypothesis, translational evidence, and the probability that a differentiated therapy can improve on existing treatment approaches. Solstice’s financing places it among the best-capitalized new oncology companies to emerge this year. Funding Details

Startup: Solstice Oncology

Investors: RA Capital Management, Canaan Partners, Forbion

Amount Raised: $225 million

Total Raised: At least $225 million disclosed

Funding Stage: Series A

Funding Date: September 9, 2026

Headquarters: Boston, Massachusetts

Sector: Biotechnology / Oncology / Immunotherapy Clay raises $115 million to expand AI-driven sales and marketing automation Clay raised $115 million in a Series D at a $7.1 billion valuation, led by Wellington Management. Reuters reported participation from Sequoia, StepStone, Andreessen Horowitz and Perennial; Axios also reported participation from a16z, Sequoia, DST Global and CapitalG. Clay develops sales and marketing software that uses AI agents to analyze company and customer data, recommend actions and execute parts of go-to-market workflows. Customers include Google and Anthropic. The valuation is the bigger story. Clay was valued at $3.1 billion in an August 2025 financing. Today’s $7.1 billion price means investors have more than doubled the mark in roughly thirteen months. That re-rating implies the market believes AI-native revenue software can take meaningful share from older sales-tech stacks rather than merely supplement them. Clay sits in one of the most contested application categories in technology. Salesforce, HubSpot, and a long list of prospecting and sales-intelligence vendors already command enterprise budgets, while new startups can access increasingly similar foundation models. Clay’s defense therefore has to come from workflow depth, integrations, proprietary customer data, user adoption, and the ability to turn fragmented sales information into actions. The funding gives it more capacity to build those advantages, but the $7.1 billion valuation sharply raises the growth expectations attached to them. Funding Details

Startup: Clay

Investors: Wellington Management, Sequoia Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, StepStone, Perennial; Axios also reports DST Global and CapitalG

Amount Raised: $115 million

Total Raised: Not disclosed in the current announcement

Funding Stage: Series D

Funding Date: September 9, 2026

Headquarters: New York, New York

Sector: Enterprise AI / Sales Technology Perry Weather raises $110 million in funding to scale automated weather safety operations Dallas-based Perry Weather secured a $110 million growth investment led by Silversmith Capital Partners, with existing investor Arthur Ventures participating. Same-day deal tracking identifies the financing as a Series C. Perry provides weather-monitoring, operations, and safety software designed to help organizations make operational decisions around weather risk. This is an easy deal to overlook beside legal AI or cybersecurity, but it reflects a durable venture theme: software is moving deeper into physical operations. Weather is not simply a forecasting problem for customers that manage outdoor workforces, facilities, sports, construction or other exposed assets; it can become a safety, liability and scheduling problem. That converts meteorological information into an operational budget rather than a consumer-information product. Silversmith’s participation is also informative. The growth investor has publicly emphasized capital-efficient technology businesses serving identifiable customer needs, and Perry fits that pattern better than a research-heavy AI bet. The investment suggests that investors still see considerable value in vertical software categories where domain specialization, embedded workflows and customer retention can matter more than model novelty. Funding Details

Startup: Perry Weather

Investors: Silversmith Capital Partners, Arthur Ventures

Amount Raised: $110 million

Total Raised: Not disclosed in the current announcement

Funding Stage: Series C / Growth financing

Funding Date: September 9, 2026

Headquarters: Dallas, Texas

Sector: Weather Technology / Operational Safety Software Savvy Wealth raises $100 million to build an AI-enabled operating platform for independent advisers Savvy Wealth raised an oversubscribed $100 million Series C at a $600 million valuation, led by Halo Fund. Thrive Capital, Industry Ventures, Canvas Prime, Index Ventures, The House Fund, Euclidean Capital, Allianz Life, Alumni Ventures and Vestigo Ventures participated. The financing takes Savvy’s disclosed capital raised to $200 million. The valuation progression is striking. In July 2025, the Financial Times reported that Savvy had raised $72 million at a $225 million valuation. A little over a year later, the company is priced at $600 million. Savvy says more than 150 advisers now use its platform, that its technology consolidates more than 20 vendors, and that advisers save an average of 19 hours per week. Those figures are company-reported, but they help explain the investor thesis: the product is trying to turn fragmented wealth-management administration into a unified operating stack. Savvy is also part of a broader convergence between venture capital and private-equity-style operating models. The FT previously reported that Savvy’s capital was being used both for technology and to acquire or recruit advisers, one example of venture firms applying software and AI to established service industries. That model can be powerful because the software has an immediate distribution channel, but it needs to prove that technology meaningfully improves economics rather than simply subsidizing asset gathering. Funding Date: September 9, 2026

Headquarters: New York, New York

Valuation: $600 million Lightfield raises $47 million to challenge traditional CRM with an AI-native system of record Lightfield announced a $47 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz, with Maverick Capital, Coatue Management, Greylock, Lightspeed, Audacious Ventures and Alumni Ventures participating. Founder Keith Peiris says more than 5,000 companies have signed up since Lightfield launched last November. The company is building an AI-native customer system that continuously draws context from interactions rather than relying solely on workers manually updating database fields. This round arrived only about two hours before the research cutoff, making it one of the freshest deals in today’s cohort. It is also one of the more strategically interesting. Traditional CRM systems were designed around human-entered records; autonomous software needs richer context, provenance, history, and permissions to act reliably. Lightfield bets that this architectural difference is large enough to support an entirely new system of record rather than another agent layered on Salesforce. The investor syndicate shows how seriously venture firms are taking that possibility. Andreessen Horowitz is joined by firms that have extensive enterprise-software experience, while Greylock and Lightspeed are also active elsewhere in the AI stack. Yet this category will be unforgiving. Clay, Salesforce, HubSpot, Attio, and numerous AI-native entrants are all chasing portions of the same revenue-operations budget. Lightfield therefore needs its accumulated customer context to become more valuable over time; otherwise, foundation-model improvements could compress differentiation. Funding Details

Funding Date: September 9, 2026

Sector: Enterprise AI / CRM / Revenue Software WINT raises $36 million in funding to expand intelligent water management WINT raised $36 million in Series D financing led by LIP Ventures and Inven Capital. Axios describes the company as a provider of water-management intelligence, positioning it at the intersection of climate technology, building operations and risk management. The deal is small relative to Harvey or Solstice, but its economics may be easier to understand than many AI application bets. Water leaks and inefficient consumption produce direct costs, property risk and insurance exposure. Software capable of detecting, analyzing and reducing those losses can therefore sell against quantifiable operational spending rather than a speculative innovation budget. That distinction matters in a venture market where investors are asking harder questions about return on AI expenditure. Climate software tied to measurable resource use can demonstrate value without relying on customers to believe a broad transformation story. The Series D stage also indicates WINT is being financed as a scaling business, not an early technology experiment. Funding Details

Startup: WINT

Investors: LIP Ventures, Inven Capital

Amount Raised: $36 million

Total Raised: Not disclosed in the current announcement

Funding Stage: Series D

Funding Date: September 9, 2026

Headquarters: New York, New York, as reported by Axios

Sector: Climate Technology / Water Intelligence Euno raises $23 million to build the context layer for enterprise AI agents Euno raised a $23 million Series A led by N47, bringing total funding to $29 million. Existing investor 10D participated alongside founders and executives associated with Wiz, Cyera, Eon, Tavily, and Tableau. Euno operates from San Francisco and Tel Aviv and is developing an enterprise “context” platform intended to reconstruct how organizational data is defined and used so AI systems can make decisions with the same institutional knowledge available to employees. The company is tackling one of enterprise AI’s less glamorous but more persistent problems: models may be able to reason over data without knowing which internal definition, metric, table, or business rule is authoritative. Companies have spent decades accumulating inconsistent schemas and undocumented assumptions. Euno’s pitch is that an AI agent needs this organizational context before it can be trusted to act autonomously across enterprise data. That puts Euno in a potentially valuable layer between models and enterprise systems, but also in a crowded part of the stack. Data platforms, catalog vendors, semantic-layer providers, and model companies are all moving toward richer context management. The investment case therefore depends on whether Euno can become a persistent knowledge layer that improves as agents work, rather than a feature that larger data platforms can replicate. Funding Details

Investors: N47, 10D, and technology-founder investors

Amount Raised: $23 million

Total Raised: $29 million

Funding Stage: Series A

Funding Date: September 9, 2026
