proofCandidates.title: The B200's rental price isn't the AI overcapacity tell
proofCandidates.summary: Nvidia's B200 GPU rental price rebounded from a June low of $4.22 to near $6.42 by September, while forward contracts and delivery lead times indicate tight supply. Forward contracts show Baseten's B200 rate jumping 94% to $5.10, and H100/A100 prices are rising, suggesting demand outpaces supply.
proofCandidates.fullText:
In late June, the hourly rental price of Nvidia's B200 GPU fell about 31% in three weeks, from a three-month high of $6.11 down to $4.22, and traders on the prediction-market platform Kalshi bet it would not get back to that high before the month was out. It was the cleanest possible version of the AI "overbuilt" fear: new capacity landing, prices collapsing, the cycle turning.

By early September the number had already turned around. The B200 spot price stood near $6.42 an hour, up about 12% over the month — and above the very peak that had triggered the panic. Older generations of the card were repricing up with it.

Here is the part the headline gets wrong. The B200 "rental price" is not the number that decides whether the AI buildout is overbuilt. It is the noisiest, most provider-dependent figure in the whole trade, and most of the time you are just watching your own index.

One chip, a dozen prices

The same physical GPU — a B200 with 192GB of HBM3e memory — rented for as little as $3.70 an hour on one neocloud in June and $14.24 an hour on a hyperscaler. That roughly 3.8x spread is not a difference in the silicon. It is provider margin, whether you are forced to buy an eight-GPU node instead of a single card, spot-versus-reserved billing, and the friction of a cloud service quota. The chip is identical in both listings.

There is no single "B200 price." Silicon Data publishes one index, Ornn another, SemiAnalysis a third, and every provider posts its own list price, and they do not agree. When a story or a title points at "the B200 rental price," it is pointing at one vendor's one index's one day's number and calling it the market.

That is a marketing-grade statistic, not an economic one.

What actually tells you the market is tight

The signal you cannot fake is the shape of the market, and on that shape the evidence points one way.

Forward contract prices are being renegotiated sharply upward, months ahead. Baseten, an AI inference provider, reported that its cloud vendors told it in May to expect its B200 rate to jump from $2.63 to $5.10 an hour at an October renewal — a 94% increase. The honest read, though, is that its baseline was a below-market rate it had locked in, and $5.10 is a catch-up to, and still slightly under, the prevailing spot. The magnitude is real, but it is "reprice to market," not "market prices double." The meaningful fact is directional: cloud providers are quoting increases months in advance, which tells you the buyer has no bargaining power.

The more durable number is delivery. Ordering roughly 1,000 GPUs now waits 12 to 15 months. That is the constraint no price index captures, because it is the supply side telling you it physically cannot meet demand on any shorter clock.

And the tell that overcapacity people keep missing: the old chips are getting more expensive, not cheaper. H100 and A100 rental rates are repricing up in 2026. If the market were flooded with surplus compute, you would be dumping last generation's hardware at a discount. Instead, new capacity is being absorbed and the installed base is holding — the pattern of demand that outruns supply, not demand that a chip shortage accidentally satisfies.

A spot price is a lagging, provider-specific snapshot. Forward contracts, delivery lead times, and the price of last generation's silicon are the leading, structural read — and all three say the compute market, as of September, is not overbuilt.

What that does — and doesn't do — to the stock

Nvidia is not the tenant here. It is the one collecting the toll. So the rental price is a second-order check on whether its customers are actually absorbing the capacity they are buying — and on this evidence, they are. NvidiaNVDA-- reported $96.2 billion in revenue for the quarter ended July 26, up 106% from a year ago, at a 75% gross margin, with a guide to roughly $108 billion next quarter. That is the ground truth. The rental market is just a downstream confirmation that the buyers are not sitting on unsold boxes.

The point for a holder or a watcher is the gap between that and the price of the stock. Nvidia trades at a forward multiple around 22x — a multiple it has not shown since before it became the AI trade — and it has slipped a few percent this month even after a record quarter. The market has already done the overcapacity math and compressed the multiple. The rental-price recovery is not what is holding the stock down, and it is not, by itself, a reason to buy. It is the removal of the main bear-case leg: the fear that a glut of Blackwell capacity would break margins. On the data, that leg is not yet broken.

Two cautions keep this from being "prices are up, therefore buy." First, a high rental price is not the same as a high return for the people renting the cards out — a neocloud quoting $5.60 an hour still destroys equity if the machines sit idle or were financed expensively, so strong prices flatter Nvidia's demand more than they prove the neoclouds are safe. Second, the one thing that would actually change this read is supply arriving ahead of that demand: if the 12- to 15-month delivery clock starts to shrink and forward prices stop firming, the "not overbuilt" verdict flips, and the rental spot price is where you would see it first. Ironically, that makes the number the headline fixates on the right early warning — even though it is the wrong thesis.

proofCandidates.title: Baseten Adds DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash to Model APIs With 1M-Token Context
proofCandidates.summary: Baseten added DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash to its Model APIs on September 11, 2026, a 552B-parameter multimodal MoE model with 1M-token context. The model scores 90.6 on Terminal-Bench and 54.8 on AutomationBench, and Baseten will route all deepseek-v4-pro requests to it starting September 14.
proofCandidates.fullText:
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is available now on Baseten Model APIs, Baseten announced on September 11, 2026, bringing the 552B-parameter multimodal mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, which pairs 8B active parameters for prefill with 16B for decode across a 1M-token context window, to the inference provider’s platform. DeepSeek released the model’s open weights on Hugging Face, and DeepSeek’s own announcement is dated September 9, 2026. The model accepts text and image input and generates text output, and the model card states that the repository and weights are licensed under the MIT License. Baseten describes V4.1-Flash as DeepSeek’s third open-weight flash release of 2026 and as the only model of its scale to use what DeepSeek calls a Causal Encoder-Decoder architecture. Support for Baseten’s Loops training product is coming soon, according to the company. Reported Benchmark Results The model card reports instruct-model results at the maximum reasoning effort setting of 100: V4.1-Flash scores 90.6 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, compared with 82.7 for V4-Flash and 87.9 for V4-Pro; 74.2 on DeepSWE v1.1, compared with 54.4 and 62.7; and 54.8 on AutomationBench, compared with 37.7 and 43.2. Baseten highlighted the same coding and agentic figures, saying V4.1-Flash beats V4-Pro with roughly a third of the total parameters, while cautioning that a 54.8 on AutomationBench means the model fails roughly half of complex workflows and advising teams to keep a human in the loop for agent pipelines. In the card’s comparison with frontier models at maximum effort, V4.1-Flash posts 90.9 on GPQA Diamond, a Codeforces rating of 3471, and 63.9 on HLE with tools. Baseten states that V4.1-Flash is DeepSeek’s first non-experimental model with native image input, a capability previously limited to the experimental V4-Flash-Vision-Exp; its table reports 78.9 on Chartography and 49 on ZeroBench for the new model, against 64.3 and 35 for the experimental one. Causal Encoder-Decoder Architecture According to the model card, V4.1-Flash organizes a 40-layer Transformer as a 20-layer causal encoder followed by a 20-layer decoder, with the decoder’s global key-value (KV) cache projected from the final encoder hidden states rather than derived from each decoder layer’s own hidden states. The design activates 8B parameters per token during prefill and 16B during decode; Baseten contrasts that with V4-Flash, which activates 13B for both steps, framing the change as trading a heavier decode for a much lighter prefill, a setup Baseten said boosts cost efficiency for coding agents whose agentic loops generate far more prefill tokens than decode tokens. The card reports that the model’s Compressed Sparse Attention 2 assigns each attention layer one of three static modes (Full, Reindex, or Reuse), with a Hierarchical Sparse Indexer in the decoder bounding deeper indexing cost independently of context length. Combined with FP4 main KV caching, those designs reduce the global KV cache to 890 bytes per token, roughly one quarter of V4-Flash, the card states. A separate mechanism, SWA Bounded Replay, reconstructs missing sliding-window-attention KV states by replaying only the most recent tokens, reducing the persistent KV footprint to roughly one eighth of V4-Flash. DeepSeek’s announcement puts the savings at one quarter the HBM and one eighth the SSD storage of the previous generation. Each MoE layer uses one shared expert and 384 routed experts with six routed experts active per token, and the model adds Engram conditional memory with 196B parameters alongside DSpark speculative decoding, according to the card. DeepSeek trained the model from scratch on a 45T-token multimodal corpus, trained its sparse attention at a 64K sequence length, and extended context to 1M tokens at 34T tokens. Post-training follows a standard supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and on-policy distillation sequence, with substantive changes concentrated in large-scale automated synthesis of agent tasks and environments, and the model exposes a continuously controllable reasoning effort setting from 1 to 100. DeepSeek API Transition and Baseten Serving DeepSeek states that V4-Flash and V4-Flash-Vision-Exp are retired on its platform, with the old API model names temporarily routing to V4.1-Flash for compatibility. New API pricing took effect at 04:00 UTC on September 10, 2026, with off-peak rates set at 50% of peak rates, and DeepSeek names official partners WorkBuddy (including CodeBuddy) and OpenCode as fully supporting V4.1-Flash. Baseten said its Inference Stack serves the model using NVIDIA Dynamo with KV cache-aware routing, steering each request to the replica already holding its prefix rather than whichever replica is free. The model is offered through Baseten’s Model Library, with dedicated deployments available for teams needing reserved capacity. Starting at 04:00 UTC on September 14, 2026, all deepseek-v4-pro requests will route to V4.1-Flash at V4.1-Flash rates, an arrangement DeepSeek said will continue until V4.1-Pro launches; the lab said tests by multiple parties put V4.1-Flash ahead of V4-Pro on performance, cost, speed, and total runtime.

Sapiom ran 2.5 million of them on Blaxel in three months. As David Zhang, founding engineer there, put it: "Blaxel handled that kind of growth in a way I'd normally expect to take a year or more to reach." Agents also produce a lot of stuff. Files, dependencies, working context, half-finished outputs. That has to outlive a single run and be reachable by the next sandbox or the next agent. Agent Drive is our distributed filesystem for that. Mount it into any sandbox and whatever an agent writes is durable, versioned, and there when something else needs it. And agents have to talk to things. Tools, MCP servers, APIs, other agents. We built the networking layer that connects sandboxes to all of that with the isolation and access controls a production team will actually sign off on. Our customers describe the result in terms we wouldn't have dared to use ourselves. Adi Singh, founder of Ara: "In our stack, alongside our auth, database, and frontend providers, the sandbox provider is the fourth pillar, and it's a new one. Blaxel is our first and most essential." The primitive we didn't own was inference. We've seen open-weight and custom models become core to how autonomous agents get deployed in production. Inference is no longer a service you call from another data center. It has to sit next to compute, storage, and network, or latency compounds on every loop. Joining Baseten is how we colocate all four. Baseten's inference stack runs at scale across dozens of regions, with more than $2B raised to build it. Together we're building the same thing from both ends: the future of agentic infrastructure. What this means for you Blaxel is continuing. The product you use today is the same product with more support behind it. The team you’ve been reaching out to for support will continue to assist you just the same. Features will keep shipping. Your API keys and credits remain valid. If anything about your setup should need to move, you’ll hear it from us first with plenty of notice. Over time, Baseten will add new products based on Blaxel’s primitives, starting with Sandboxes. Together with inference and training, these primitives will be the foundation for the agentic infrastructure we’re building. What’s shipping next The roadmap is full and we only plan on increasing our shipping velocity. On the compute side, we’re rolling out Carbon (aka Mk 3.1), our new generation of compute runtime, which is our most important upgrade we’ve done on the product since we launched sandboxes. The Carbon runtime unlocks many long-awaited features: sandbox checkpointing (so you can rollback a sandbox state at a point in time), forking (so that your agents can explore parallel universes in sandboxes – or simply to create already running sandboxes faster), and dedicated IPv6 for every sandbox. On the storage side, Blaxel Agent Drive now has an S3 API, so you can read and write files directly from the outside world. We’re rolling it out in Europe, and improving performances every week. On the networking side, we recently added custom functions and method matching to Blaxel Proxy. Next, we’re unlocking full extensibility with custom plugins and extensions. Across the products, reliability is our north star. We intend to serve the next trillion agents. The people stay the people My co-founders Charles, Mathis, Chris, Nico, and the rest of the team you talk to daily remain the same people. They will be doing the same work, with more support behind them. Feel free to reach out to us if you have any questions about this acquisition. Most importantly: thank you. You made a bet on our infrastructure early, and you’ve shaped the product with your feedback. We don’t take that lightly. If you have a question about any of this, contact us directly on our Discord or your traditional point of contact. We’re happy to talk.

proofCandidates.title: Baseten buys Blaxel, a startup that builds sandboxes for AI agents
proofCandidates.summary: Baseten acquired Blaxel, a San Francisco startup that builds secure execution environments for AI agents. Blaxel's sandboxes spin up and resume up to five times faster than competing products, with suspend/resume in 25 milliseconds. Baseten will add new products based on Blaxel's technology, starting with sandboxes.
proofCandidates.fullText:
AI inference company Baseten has acquired Blaxel, a startup that builds secure execution environments, or sandboxes, for AI agents. Baseten co-founder and chief technology officer Amir Haghighat told Axios Pro about the deal, which the outlet reported first on Thursday. Baseten later announced the acquisition.

Axios describes Blaxel as a San Francisco startup. The announcement did not disclose financial terms.

What Blaxel builds

Blaxel builds sandboxes based on microVMs, small isolated virtual machines. Each agent gets its own. According to the release, the sandboxes spin up and resume up to five times faster than competing products.

In a joint blog post, the companies said a Blaxel sandbox can suspend and resume in 25 milliseconds. It can also sit idle for months at close to zero cost.

Its other products include Agent Drive, a distributed filesystem that agents can share, and a networking layer that connects agents to tools, MCP servers, APIs and other agents. The team has been building the platform for more than 18 months, the post said.

What changes for customers

According to the post, Blaxel will continue to operate and its product does not change. Baseten will add new products based on Blaxel’s technology, starting with sandboxes.

In the near term, Blaxel’s technology expands Baseten’s support for code execution, tool use and session persistence, the release said. Over time, Baseten plans to integrate it with its inference, storage, observability and enterprise infrastructure.

“Agents need models, but they also need a secure environment to run in that’s fast, scalable, and reliable enough for production,” Haghighat said in the release.

Paul Sinaï, Blaxel’s co-founder and chief executive, said: “We started Blaxel because agents need environments designed to work alongside the models powering them.”

Baseten’s run of deals

Baseten, founded in 2019, has raised more than $2bn. In June, TNW reported that it raised $1.5bn at up to $13bn. The release puts the valuation of that Series F round at $13bn.

In December 2025, Baseten acquired Parsed, a reinforcement learning startup. Its customers include Abridge, Clay, Cursor, Lovable, Mercor and OpenEvidence, according to the company.

proofCandidates.summary: Blaxel is joining Baseten to build a unified agentic infrastructure platform. Blaxel provides stateful execution with microVM sandboxes and persistent storage, while Baseten offers inference. proofCandidates.fullText:
Today, Blaxel is joining Baseten. By joining forces, we aim to build the cloud for the next trillion agents. Baseten has built the infrastructure that teams use to train and serve models with industry-leading performance, reliability, and efficiency. Blaxel has built the stateful execution layer agents need to act: fast, isolated sandboxes, persistent storage, and production-grade connectivity. Together, we are expanding Baseten into the infrastructure foundation where teams can serve and train models and can now build long-running agents, all in one integrated platform. Both companies were founded with the conviction that AI would become ubiquitous and require a new generation of infrastructure. Baseten was started with the belief that delivering fast, reliable inference at scale would become a defining bottleneck to AI adoption. Blaxel was founded on the belief that existing clouds weren't designed for how AI agents run and couldn't support them at scale. For more than 18 months, we at Blaxel have been building this new cloud, one primitive at a time. Sandboxes came first because nothing else works without them. Agents write and run code, call tools, and carry state across long tasks, and you can't do that safely in a shared process. Every agent gets its own microVM. We made them extremely fast: suspend and resume in 25 milliseconds, up to 5x faster than other sandbox products. A sandbox can sit idle for months at close to zero cost and come back before the model finishes its next sentence, so state persists without paying for compute you aren't using.

Sapiom runs hundreds of millions of agent loops on Blaxel. As David Zhang, founding engineer there, put it: "Blaxel handled that kind of growth in a way I'd normally expect to take a year or more to reach." Agents also need to persist and share many artifacts: files, code, and working context. That has to outlive a single run and be accessible to the next sandbox or agent. Agent Drive is our distributed filesystem for that. Mount it into any sandbox and whatever an agent writes is durable, versioned, and there when something else needs it. And agents have to talk to things. Tools, MCP servers, APIs, other agents. We rebuilt a networking layer that connects all of these pieces with the isolation and access controls a production team will actually sign off on. The primitive we didn't own was inference. We've seen open-weight & custom models become core to how autonomous agents get deployed in production. Inference is no longer a service you call from another data center. It has to sit next to compute, storage, and network; or latency compounds on every loop. That brings us to Baseten – joining forces is how we colocate all four, bringing the brain next to the muscles. Baseten's inference stack is the best on the market, running at scale across dozens of regions, with more than $2B raised to build it. Our shared vision is a future where many agents use many models at massive scale across every part of our daily lives. Together, we’ll build the infrastructure layer that lets millions of autonomous agents run safely with the best performance, reliability, and economics possible. Why Blaxel and Baseten When our teams first met, we each believed running agents at scale meant more than a great sandbox solution or a great inference solution. As conversations progressed and we continued to share learnings, however, it became clear that the best solution was to operate as closely together as possible. The decision worked because we made the same architectural bets based on the same shared beliefs about the market. We had just done it from different parts of the stack. Both companies built from the ground up for what it would take to truly scale the workload to our customers’ requirements, rather than taking the fastest path to market. We had both decided that performance, reliability, scalability, security, flexibility, and cost-efficiency needed to be first-class considerations. And we each believed customers need maximum visibility, control, and ownership. And customers confirm this. As Utkarsh Sengar, CTO of Webflow, put it: "You guys helped us bring a lot of reliability in our system.” For us, the most important point is that this massively accelerates our vision. We are bringing together two highly complementary companies at exactly the right moment as the market takes shape. Together we're building a platform where agent execution, inference, and training run on one system. Agents act next to the models they're calling, not across a network boundary. Persistent environments that carry state across turns and sessions. Post-training runs that write to the same storage layer the sandbox reads from, so improving a model on what its agents actually did is part of the same system.

We give them the cloud infrastructure they need, highly configurable and delivered at the velocity they require, in milliseconds. Today, this means building around what customers care about most: speed, uptime, and economics. The teams that win will not be the ones running the most agents; they’ll be the ones whose agents are most efficient and improve fastest. What this means for our customers Blaxel is continuing. The team you've been reaching out to for support will continue to assist you just the same as always. The product doesn't change, and features will keep shipping. Over time, Baseten will add new products based on Blaxel's primitives, starting with Sandboxes. Together with inference and training, these new primitives will be the foundation for the agentic infrastructure we're building. Charles, Mathis, Chris, Nico, and the rest of the team you talk to daily remain the same people, doing the same work, with more behind them. Most importantly, we’re grateful for the trust you've placed in us. You made a bet on our infrastructure early and have shaped the product with your feedback. We don't take that lightly, and we thank you for it!

proofCandidates.title: Baseten Acquires Blaxel to Build the Infrastructure for AI Agents in Production
proofCandidates.summary: Baseten acquired Blaxel, an infrastructure company building secure, persistent execution environments for AI agents. Blaxel's microVM-based sandboxes spin up and resume up to 5x faster than competitive solutions. The acquisition expands Baseten's platform toward a complete runtime for production AI applications.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Baseten Acquires Blaxel to Build the Infrastructure for AI Agents in Production
Baseten Acquires Blaxel to Build the Infrastructure for AI Agents in Production
The acquisition expands Baseten’s ability to deliver perpetual sandbox execution in the same production platform customers already use for inference, training, and post-training
SAN FRANCISCO--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Baseten, the AI inference company powering the world's most advanced AI applications, today announced that it has acquired Blaxel, an infrastructure company building secure, persistent execution environments, or sandboxes, for AI agents. With the acquisition, Blaxel joins Baseten, bringing deep expertise and technology for agentic tools and infrastructure. Together with Blaxel, Baseten further expands its platform toward delivering the fastest, most reliable, secure and cost-effective infrastructure agents need to run code, use tools and maintain state.
"AI applications have moved from models that generate answers to agents that actually do things," said Amir Haghighat, co-founder and CTO of Baseten. "Agents need models, but they also need a secure environment to run in that's fast, scalable, and reliable enough for production. Adding Blaxel to Baseten will accelerate our vision to provide the infrastructure and tooling for agents to reliably operate, with great performance, at scale."
AI applications are increasingly taking actions instead of just generating responses, creating new infrastructure requirements. For security and efficiency, these agentic workloads require isolated execution environments that can persist across long-running tasks without creating unnecessary overhead.
Blaxel has built infrastructure specifically for this emerging class of applications, including secure microVM-based sandboxes that spin up and resume up to 5x faster than competitive sandbox solutions. The platform natively supports agent code execution, tool use, MCP servers, and other workloads that require secure, stateful compute.
By bringing Blaxel’s execution infrastructure together with Baseten’s inference platform, Baseten is building toward a more complete runtime for production AI applications. Developers will be able to run models and the environments where those models act on infrastructure designed to work together, cutting down the latency and complexity that comes from moving state and data between separate systems.
Paul Sinaï, co-founder and CEO of Blaxel, said: “We started Blaxel because agents need environments designed to work alongside the models powering them. Bringing Blaxel together with Baseten means we can build for where we think the infrastructure is headed for agents in production: a model and execution environment in a single system.”
In the near term, Blaxel’s technology expands Baseten’s foundation for secure code execution, tool use and session persistence. Over time, these capabilities will be integrated more deeply with Baseten’s inference, storage, observability and enterprise infrastructure to strengthen its support for agentic workflows.
The acquisition follows a period of significant expansion for Baseten, including a Series F fundraise with a $13 billion valuation and the acquisition of Parsed, the reinforcement learning startup specialized in post-training and continual learning.
About Baseten
Baseten is the inference company behind a new generation of AI products. The company builds systems software that runs the entire workload for AI applications—from GPUs and autoscaling to observability, billing, and developer tools—so teams can focus on models and user experience instead of infrastructure. Baseten’s customers include leading AI companies such as Abridge, Clay, Cursor, Lovable, Mercor, and OpenEvidence and others building specialized models for their domains. Founded in 2019 and based in San Francisco, Baseten has raised over $2 billion to date from investors including Altimeter Capital, Battery Ventures, Blackbird, BOND, CapitalG, Conviction, Durable Capital Partners, Greylock, IVP, NVIDIA, Sands Capital, Spark Capital, Verified Capital, Wellington Management, 01A and others.

proofCandidates.title: I Went to a Private Longevity Night Hosted by Bryan Johnson
proofCandidates.summary: Baseten hosted a private longevity night with Bryan Johnson and Sarah Guo, drawing over 3,000 applicants for 100 slots. Attendees took bioage tests and a Q&A, with Johnson noting he might have taken longevity too far. He said he gives permission to revel in the joy of dying.
proofCandidates.fullText:
The only topic these days that gets people in San Francisco to stop talking about AI is living forever.

When Baseten, an AI startup (what else?), announced a few weeks ago, it was hosting a "private evening" with tech entrepreneur and longevity evangelist Bryan Johnson and VC Sarah Guo at its SF office, over 3,000 people applied to get in for just 100 slots.

For the uninitiated, Johnson made hundreds of millions selling his payment startup to PayPal and now spends millions a year on a wellness regime that he shares with his 2.7 million Instagram followers. Johnson has been in the news a lot this summer, after he revealed he has autoimmune gastritis, an incurable chronic condition of the stomach. Then, last month, he said, "he might have taken 'this whole longevity thing too far."

When I arrived, the registration table was swarmed by people condemned to the waitlist trying to angle their way in.

"Don't bother," said the person at the desk. "It's full."

Once I squeezed past the crowds, I was handed a color-coded schedule with three stations: Breathwork, Bioage tests, and a Q&A with Dr. Carl Seger , Johnson's lead doctor.

"Nothing you measure tonight is a verdict," I was told. "It's a baseline, and every one of these markers can be moved."

The Tumeric Elixir Ben Bergman/Business Insider

But first, it was time for happy hour! No hors d'oeuvres or wine here. Instead, can I interest you in raw vegetables and mocktails to take the edge off? I opted for a refreshing "Tumeric Elixir" with orange juice, carrot juice, ginger, and tumeric.

As soon as I walked in, I noticed everyone seemed overwhelmingly youthful. One tech founder in his fifties told me he felt ancient. So either Johnson's routine is working wonders or this crowd was emblematic of Silicon Valley's "youthquake."

I asked an enthusiastic young machine learning engineer who works at Uber why he was there.

"Bryan Johnson is just so cool!" he said.

But enough chitchat. It was time to get my face scanned to learn my "face age." After a few minutes, a reading popped up. I was in the 80th percentile for wrinkles (which is apparently very good), but my "face age" was older than my real age.

The author getting a "face age" scan Ben Bergman/Business Insider

Feeling a little dejected, I walked over to the bioage stations, where participants underwent a series of tests, such as grip strength, push-ups, and a one-leg stand, to measure their biological age. Johnson, accompanied by his new guard dog, Katara, strode by, playfully encouraging people to do a few more push-ups.

A few feet away, engineers were coding on giant screens. We were in an office after all, not a gym, and the work must go on.

Before Johnson's interview, it was time for a dinner "guided" by his personal chef, Tara Amanya. There were box meals with chicken and vegetables, but I opted for the salmon, which was tasty but left me a bit hungry.

A salmon dinner "guided" by Bryan Johnson's personal chef Ben Bergman/Business Insider

Anything that gets people to exercise more or eat healthier should be commended. Still, I was struck by how many questions throughout the night came down to people wanting easy shortcuts to essentially hack life, as if it were an algorithm to be exploited.

Again and again, people kept asking: "What is the one thing I can do to live longer?"

I kept thinking about my grandparents, who never heard of peptides or biohacking. They drank wine with dinner every night and mostly ate whatever they wanted. They all lived well into their nineties.

Sarah Guo from Conviction Capital interviews Bryan Johnson Ben Bergman/Business Insider

Johnson is far more self-aware than he can seem on Instagram, and when he was interviewed by Guo to end the evening, he said: "We all know I'm going to die, but it's going to be being hit by a bus or choking on broccoli."

"I give you permission to revel in the joy of it," he continued. "That is irony, and my ultimate foe is irony."

After the talk ended, I walked back to my hotel and ordered a chocolate chip cookie.

Do you have a tip about life in Silicon Valley? Contact reporter Ben Bergman securely on Signal at @BenBergman.11

proofCandidates.title: Writer bets on cheaper AI agents with Palmyra X6 and a leaner harness
proofCandidates.summary: Writer launched Palmyra X6, a post-training GLM-5.2 model, with a harness that optimizes token usage. The company claims up to 50% cost savings for basic tasks, with harness efficiency alone trimming costs by about 40%. The harness is model-agnostic, working with Azure and Bedrock.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Writer, the enterprise AI company, has launched Palmyra X6, its new flagship model, alongside an upgraded “harness” built to do something the industry has been curiously reluctant to promise: spend fewer tokens.
The model is a post-training variation on Z.ai’s open-source GLM-5.2, and it is available to Writer’s clients from today.
The pitch arrives at a nervy moment. As agentic AI quietly multiplies the steps, and therefore the tokens, behind every task, enterprise bills have started to sting.
Writer is wagering that a cost backlash has arrived, and it is far from alone in scenting the opportunity, with Baseten raising $1.5bn on the theory that AI’s profits lie in cheap inference.
A harness, in Writer’s telling, is the orchestration layer wrapped around a model, the machinery that decides how a multi-step agent actually executes each request.
Optimise that layer, trimming the redundant calls and bloated context that agents tend to accumulate, and you cut token consumption without ever touching the model itself.
The savings, Writer says, are substantial. The company estimates that the new model and harness together cut costs by as much as 50% for basic tasks, while a Writer research paper found that harness-efficiency changes alone trimmed costs by roughly 40% on average across testing.
What makes the harness interesting is that it is model-agnostic. It works with Writer’s own models, but also with external ones served through Microsoft Azure and Amazon Bedrock, so the efficiency gains are not locked to a single vendor’s roadmap.
“The harness is the one component whose efficiency multiplies across every model an organization runs, present and future,” Writer’s researchers write, framing orchestration rather than raw model quality as the lever enterprises have been ignoring.
It is also a pointed one. Writer’s underlying claim is that the big labs have little incentive to help you spend less, because their revenue rises with every token you burn. Distrust of that arrangement is doing a lot of work in the company’s messaging.
CEO May Habib put it bluntly. “The enterprise is absolutely sick of chasing the next benchmark,” she said. “They want flattening cost.” It is a neat inversion of the usual sales script, in which each new model is faster, cleverer and, invariably, hungrier.
A wider thrift-maxxing trend, in which buyers reach for cheaper Chinese models, has already started to unsettle the valuations underpinning eventual OpenAI and Anthropic IPOs, a sign that price sensitivity is no longer a fringe concern.
Building the flagship on GLM-5.2 is telling in its own right. Rather than train a frontier model from scratch, Writer took a capable open-source base and specialised it through post-training, a route that keeps costs down and neatly matches the frugal story it is selling.
For European buyers, the framing should feel familiar. Scepticism about American hyperscalers’ incentives, and a preference for architectures that are not hostage to one provider, has been a running theme on this side of the Atlantic, and Writer is pitching straight into it.
There are caveats worth keeping in mind. Efficiency figures produced by a vendor about its own product deserve the usual pinch of salt, and “up to” 50% is not the same as a guaranteed 50%, but the direction of travel is hard to dispute.
The deeper shift is what Writer calls harness engineering: the discipline of spending fewer tokens per task rather than chasing another point on a leaderboard. If it takes hold, and the incentives increasingly suggest it will, the era of the ever-hungrier model may finally be meeting its budget.

NEW YORK , Aug. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- WhiteFiber, Inc. (Nasdaq: WYFI) ("WhiteFiber" or the "Company"), a leading provider of AI infrastructure and high-performance computing solutions, today announced financial results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. Sam Tabar, Chief Executive Officer of WhiteFiber, said: "At NC-1, we moved from construction into active customer deployment. Initial billing has commenced, and we expect to reach full contracted run-rate billing across the 40 megawatts of contracted IT load later this month. NC-1 is our flagship site and demonstrates our ability to acquire and develop large-scale AI infrastructure, with the potential to scale toward approximately 300 gross megawatts over time. We have entered into exclusivity with a consortium of lenders for a proposed secured financing for NC-1. We are progressing through diligence and are negotiating definitive documentation. This potential financing is subject to customary approvals and conditions, and we cannot provide assurance that the financing will be completed on favorable terms or at all. However, if completed, we expect this financing would return a significant portion of our invested capital to the balance sheet and allow us to recycle it into future development. The repositioning of our Cloud Services business around larger, longer-duration engagements is translating into meaningful momentum. Since our last earnings call, we have signed new multi-year agreements representing more than half a billion dollars of aggregate contract value over their initial terms. These include NVIDIA B300 deployments with Baseten, our first Vera Rubin deployment with Prime Intellect and our previously announced five-year deployment in the Paris region. We are also seeing strong customer interest in a capital-light managed-services offering through which customers would fund the underlying hardware while WhiteFiber deploys and operates it. Our development pipeline continues to advance, with our next opportunity now in late-stage diligence. Power available at scale in 2027 is scarce, and we are seeing strong demand, including from opportunities that include investment-grade credit support. We believe this combination can support attractive economics and financeability, and we are focused on converting the opportunity into a definitive agreement on the right terms. NC-1 is generating revenue, our contracted Cloud Services portfolio has expanded substantially, and our next phase of development is coming into focus. We believe WhiteFiber is now beginning to demonstrate the development flywheel we set out to build." proofCandidates.title: WYFI Stock Rallies On Earnings Beat, CEO Says NC-1 Has Entered ‘Active Customer Deployment’ With Initial Billing Underway
proofCandidates.summary: WhiteFiber reported second-quarter revenue of $28.8 million, exceeding analyst estimates, while announcing that its flagship NC-1 data center has entered active customer deployment with initial billing underway. The company also disclosed signing over $500 million in new multi-year Cloud Services agreements with clients including Baseten and Prime Intellect for GPU deployments across North America and Europe. Consequently, WhiteFiber's shares rallied approximately 13% in pre-market trading following the earnings beat and positive operational updates.
proofCandidates.fullText:
WhiteFiber reported $28.8 million in second-quarter revenue, above the $18 million analyst estimate.

On Monday, Deutsche Bank said CAR’s downgrade to ‘Hold’ from ‘Buy' is "purely fundamental in nature"

CEO Sam Tabar said NC-1 has moved "from construction into active customer deployment," with initial billing underway and full contracted run-rate billing expected later this month.

Tabar added that WhiteFiber has signed more than $500 million of new multi-year Cloud Services agreements since its previous earnings call.

He also stated that the company is pursuing secured financing for NC-1 and seeing customer interest in a capital-light model.

Shares of WhiteFiber (WYFI) rallied in pre-market trade on Wednesday after the AI infrastructure company reported a second-quarter beat and its CEO said that “initial billing” was underway at its flagship NC-1 data center campus.

CEO Sam Tabar said WhiteFiber has moved NC-1 "from construction into active customer deployment." “Initial billing has commenced, and we expect to reach full contracted run-rate billing across the 40 megawatts of contracted IT load later this month,” he added.

WYFI stock gained around 13% in pre-market trade and was among the top trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing.

WhiteFiber reported second-quarter (Q2) revenue of $28.8 million, topping the $18 million analysts’ estimate cited by Koyfin. Loss per share came in at $0.39, compared with expectations of a $0.40 per share loss.

WhiteFiber’s New AI Contracts Top $500M

Since the company’s previous earnings call in May, Tabar stated WhiteFiber has signed new multi-year Cloud Services agreements representing more than $500 million of aggregate contract value over their initial terms.

“Since our last earnings call, we have signed new multi-year agreements representing more than half a billion dollars of aggregate contract value over their initial terms,” he stated.

The agreements include a $165 million deal with Baseten to deploy 1,392 NVIDIA B300 GPUs in Ontario and a $108 million agreement with Prime Intellect covering 576 NVIDIA VR200 GPUs in Canada.

WhiteFiber also signed a five-year agreement worth more than $160 million for a GPU deployment in the Paris region and an $87.5 million agreement for 576 NVIDIA B300 GPUs in Iceland.

WhiteFiber Moves NC-1 Into Customer Deployment

Tabar stated that NC-1 has the potential to scale toward approximately 300 gross megawatts over time. He added that WhiteFiber is also pursuing secured financing for the project and has entered into exclusivity with a consortium of lenders.

"We are also seeing strong customer interest in a capital-light managed-services offering through which customers would fund the underlying hardware while WhiteFiber deploys and operates it,” Tabar said. He explained that the approach could allow the company to expand its AI infrastructure business without bearing the full upfront cost of the GPU hardware.

“We believe WhiteFiber is now beginning to demonstrate the development flywheel we set out to build,” Tabar stated.

How Is Retail Feeling About WYFI Stock?

On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around WYFI stock improved to ‘neutral’ from ‘extremely bearish’ territory, while chatter rose to ‘normal’ from ‘low’ levels. Platform data showed that message volume had more than doubled in the last 24 hours.

WYFI stock retail sentiment on August 12 as of 8:00 a.m. ET | Source: Stocktwits

One retail trader highlighted the low float of WYFI stock, indicating that the stock has the potential to hold its rally if the Consumer Price Index (CPI) data comes in cool.

dssblue $WYFI Heavily shorted! Tiny float 38M shares. If CPI comes in cool today will be fun 🚀

However, another retail investor flagged their concern about the approximately $230 million of convertible notes, with a conversion price of $25.91.

Disrupter $WYFI My only concern is $230M convertables at conversion price of $25.91

WYFI stock has gained more than 56% so far this year.

code: chief_executive_officer
label: Chief Executive Officer
name: Tuhin Srivastava
overview: Co-founder and CEO of Baseten, leading the AI inference infrastructure company's strategic direction and growth since co-founding the firm in 2019.
profile commentary: Tuhin Srivastava co-founded Baseten in 2019 alongside Amir Haghighat, Philip Howes, and Pankaj Gupta and has served as CEO since inception. Under his leadership, Baseten scaled from a $20M seed/Series A round in 2022 to a $1.5B Series F at a $13B valuation by June 2026, growing revenue approximately 20x year-over-year to an annualized run-rate approaching $1 billion in 2026. He is the public voice of the company, frequently quoted in major outlets (WSJ, Forbes, Reuters, VentureBeat, TechCrunch) and appearing on industry podcasts such as the AI Compute podcast to discuss inference as the bottleneck in AI deployment. He has guided the company through the December 2025 acquisition of Parsed (a reinforcement learning startup) and the strategic $150M investment from NVIDIA in January 2026, positioning Baseten as the partner of choice for AI-native companies shipping production AI products.
source: https://www.startuphub.ai/ai-news/artificial-intelligence/2026/ai-compute-the-bottleneck-for-startup-scaling

As a co-founder, he contributes to the technical and strategic direction of the AI inference platform that has grown to process over one billion inference calls daily across 87 clusters and 18 cloud providers worldwide.

proofCandidates.fullText:
core offering: Baseten provides an AI inference platform that enables businesses to deploy, optimize, and scale open-source, custom, and fine-tuned AI models in production. The Baseten Inference Stack combines custom model runtimes, custom kernels, advanced caching, the latest decoding techniques, and multi-cloud capacity management across 18-20 cloud providers and 87 clusters globally. Offerings include Dedicated Deployments for custom models, pre-optimized Model APIs, Training infrastructure, and the Frontier Gateway for white-label inference APIs, supported by Forward Deployed Engineers for hands-on customer support.
differentiator: 1) Most performant inference at scale via the Baseten Inference Stack with custom kernels, custom runtimes, advanced caching, and the latest decoding techniques — validated by independent benchmarks (NVIDIA-cited 4-10x cost reductions on Blackwell). 2) Multi-cloud, multi-region capacity across ~18-20 cloud providers and 87 clusters, enabling scale-from-zero autoscaling with 99.999% uptime. 3) End-to-end platform combining dedicated deployments, Model APIs, Training, Embeddings Inference, and Frontier Gateway under one roof. 4) Forward Deployed Engineers (FDE) embedded with strategic customers, enabling companies without ML teams to deploy production AI. 5) Open-source model specialization rather than building base models — serves the open-weight ecosystem with optimized open-source alternatives to closed APIs. 6) Own your intelligence thesis: helps companies build systems shaped by proprietary data, evals, domain-specific harnesses, post-training, and custom RL environments rather than renting from closed providers.
functional benefit: Fastest model runtimes, cross-cloud high availability, seamless developer workflows, fast cold starts (5-10 seconds), low latency (sub-250ms p90), high reliability (99.999% uptime), major cost reductions (4-10x vs proprietary alternatives, 65%+ vs competitors), ability to own proprietary data and models, post-training research support.
problem solved: Inference has become the critical bottleneck for AI deployment as the industry shifts from model training to production deployment. Baseten solves the gap between frontier model availability and production-ready inference — providing the fastest model runtimes, cross-cloud high availability, fine-tuning, embeddings, transcription, image generation, and managed gateways on a single platform, enabling companies to deploy open-source and custom models at scale with predictable cost, latency, and reliability.
quantifiable outcome: OpenEvidence achieved 78% lower latency (160ms end-to-end), 6x faster deployment, 8x+ reduction in maintenance hours
quantifiable outcome: Gamma achieved 30-80% faster image generation, 20% improved efficiency, scaled to 70M+ users with lean 50-person team, $100M+ ARR, 3M+ images generated daily
quantifiable outcome: EliseAI achieved 60% reduction in inference cost, 80% reduction in latency, 250ms p90 latency (from 2.2s), 99% accuracy on 4B parameter model
quantifiable outcome: Hebbia achieved 2.5x improvement in tokens per second, 4x improvement in time to first token, 10x+ inference cost reduction
quantifiable outcome: Speechify cut costs by 44%, reduced p99 latency by 30-50%, achieved 4.5x faster cold starts, synthesizing 161B+ characters per month for 60M+ users
quantifiable outcome: Sully.ai achieved 90% cost reduction on Blackwell GPUs using NVFP4 format, handling 30M clinical minutes
quantifiable outcome: Latitude achieved 75% cost reduction on Blackwell via NVFP4 quantization
quantifiable outcome: Decagon achieved 6x cost reduction on Blackwell GPUs
quantifiable outcome: Zed Industries serves 2x faster code completions with Baseten
quantifiable outcome: OpenEvidence embeddings inference achieved 3x speed improvements, 160ms latency
quantifiable outcome: Some customers reduced AI spending to roughly 30% of proprietary model costs
quantifiable outcome: Baseten itself grew revenue 20x year-over-year and inference volume 40x
quantifiable outcome: Clickup achieved sub-300ms transcription latency with no unpredictable spikes
product overview: Baseten offers a unified AI inference platform with a platform-plus-modules architecture centered on the Baseten Inference Stack, which combines the fastest model runtimes, cross-cloud high availability, and seamless developer workflows. The platform encompasses core products Dedicated Inference (for high-scale workloads serving open-source, custom, and fine-tuned models), Model APIs (pre-optimized model endpoints with pay-per-token pricing), Training (for owning model weights with one-click deployment), and Frontier Gateway (managed gateway for AI model labs to deploy white-labeled production inference APIs), supported by deployment options (Baseten Cloud, Self-hosted, and Hybrid), platform modules including Multi-cloud Capacity Management (MCM), Baseten Chains for compound AI, and Baseten Embeddings Inference (BEI), plus the open-source Truss framework and the acquired Parsed post-training capabilities. Together these offerings let customers deploy, optimize, and manage AI models with exceptional latency, reliability, observability, and cost at production scale across more than 15 cloud providers.

proofCandidates.title: Why AI Compute Comes in Rectangles — Erik Bernhardsson, Modal CEO — Latent Space
proofCandidates.summary: Modal CEO Erik Bernhardsson discussed the company's growth, including a $750 million Series D at a $16B valuation and nearly three billion sandboxes. He explained that GPU demand is irregular, not rectangular, and that sandboxes now account for about a third of revenue. He also noted the risk of GPU prices falling if capacity is locked in.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Warm welcome to Basil Chatha, our newest cohost from the Forward Deployed side of the AI Engineering world! We’ll be ramping up a new show with him and couldn’t pass up an interview with Modal’s CEO Eric on the occasion of their monster Series D! Two years ago, we spoke with Erik Bernhardsson about his vision for truly serverless AI infrastructure: developers should be able to run code without provisioning clusters, predicting load, or paying for idle resources. CTO Akshat then joined us to talk about Modal’s infra primitives and stack to offer those primitives and agent experience. A lot has changed in the past 5 months. Since their $5B series C, Modal now reports it crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate, raised a $750 million Series D at a $16B valuation, and has spun up nearly three billion sandboxes. In this conversation, Erik joins Vibhu to explain the infrastructure and economics behind that growth—and why demand for compute rarely looks like the contracts used to buy it. Watch the full conversation on YouTube → GPU demand isn’t rectangular A typical capacity contract gives a customer a fixed number of GPUs for a fixed period. Plot capacity against time and you get a rectangle. Real workloads behave differently: they grow, spike, and fall throughout the day. Buy enough for the peak and you pay for idle hardware; buy less and you risk missing demand. Erik describes Modal’s bet as a kind of duration transformation: pool demand across thousands of customers, secure capacity underneath, and let each customer use what they need when they need it. The smoother the aggregate demand, the more useful that pool can be. It’s a useful companion to our conversation with SF Compute’s Evan Conrad: Evan focuses on making capacity tradeable; Erik focuses on making it usable in smaller, elastic slices. There is a financial risk on the other side. If a provider locks in capacity at today’s prices and GPU prices later fall, it can be left holding expensive supply. Erik says he doesn’t expect an imminent collapse, but thinks the possibility matters when building the business. Jump to the GPU price discussion → The sandbox that almost didn’t make it Modal launched sandboxes after Erik and cofounder Akshat Bubna noticed that language models could generate code—and that someone would need a place to run it. Early adoption was modest enough that the team discussed shutting the product down. Then coding agents, background agents, and reinforcement learning created new demand. Erik says sandboxes have grown to roughly a third of Modal’s revenue, a result he didn’t predict at launch. That growth also changes what infrastructure has to do. An agent may create an environment, run code, inspect the result, and try again many times. The latency of starting and restoring those environments becomes part of the experience. In our recent interview with Akshat, we explored this shift from developer experience to agent experience; here Erik adds the product and business story. Jump to the sandbox discussion → Fast startup is an infrastructure feature Elasticity only works if capacity can arrive quickly enough to matter. Modal’s serverless GPU write-up describes the machinery: a buffer of available GPUs, a custom filesystem, process checkpointing, and GPU memory snapshots. Those pieces reduce the work needed to bring another model replica online. It is a concrete example of how infrastructure decisions show up in an application’s responsiveness and cost. We also discuss Erik’s path from Spotify’s recommendation system to Modal, how the company buys compute, alternatives to NVIDIA, forward-deployed engineers, and why code review is optional at Modal. proofCandidates.title: Nvidia wins fast-growing AI startup Modal for new central processors
proofCandidates.summary: Modal, an AI cloud-computing startup, will adopt Nvidia's Vera central processor for hosting AI agents, after raising $750 million at a $15.75 billion valuation. The company expects $1 billion in sales next year and will run Nvidia chips alongside Intel and AMD in a mixed fleet.
proofCandidates.fullText:
- Artificial Intelligence
- 2 min read
Nvidia wins fast-growing AI startup Modal for new central processors
Modal, a cloud-computing startup dedicated to AI development, has partnered with Nvidia to adopt their new Vera chip, transitioning away from Intel and AMD processors. This strategic shift comes after raising $750 million in funding, boosting Modal's valuation to $15.75 billion. The company has also reported substantial revenue growth over the past year and will continue to explore additional hardware options as they arise.
Nvidia has won central processor chip business with another fast-growing AI startup that until now relied entirely on chips from Intel and AMD, an early sign that its push into a market long controlled by those two rivals has traction.
Modal, a cloud-computing startup that rents out computing power to AI developers, said it plans to start using Nvidia's new Vera central processor for the first time for hosting agents, the AI systems that can carry out long-running tasks for human users. Modal until now has run such work only on Intel and AMD chips.
Modal last week raised $750 million in a funding round led by Accel at a $15.75 billion valuation, saying it is on track to record $1 billion in sales over the next year. Modal said usage of its services has tripled and revenue has grown more than 15 times year-over-year.
Modal said Monday that early tests showed the new Nvidia chip doubled the amount of work that AI agents can get done, prompting the company to support Nvidia's chip design for the first time, which will require some deep software changes on Modal's side.
But Chief Executive Erik Bernhardsson was careful to stress it is not abandoning its existing suppliers. The company said it will run the Nvidia chips alongside its current Intel and AMD offerings in a mixed fleet, putting each job on whatever hardware runs it best.
Bernhardsson said the tests were run against the Intel and AMD chips already on the market. Both Nvidia rivals are developing newer models that could narrow the gap with Nvidia.
"We'll test them when they're available," he said, adding that running a mixed setup means the company "can always deploy whatever hardware performs best."
Nvidia has told investors it expects to generate at least $20 billion from Vera chip sales this fiscal year, its opening bid for a market it values at roughly $200 billion. Nvidia has previously said OpenAI, Anthropic and Oracle also plan to use the chips, along with AI startups such as Perplexity.

proofCandidates.title: Modal taps Nvidia Vera CPUs after firm's internal tests show 2x throughput over Intel and AMD chips — AI agentic workflows said to favor Arm chips, but firm will keep x86 chips deployed in heterogeneo
proofCandidates.summary: Nvidia's Vera CPUs delivered twice the throughput of AMD and Intel processors in Modal's tests, but Modal will keep x86 chips in a heterogeneous fleet. Modal expects $1 billion in annual revenue within a year, and Nvidia expects Vera sales to generate at least $20 billion this fiscal year.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Nvidia has earned billions selling AI accelerators, but with the emergence of agentic AI, CPUs are going to play a considerably more significant role than before, which creates new opportunities for the company. Reuters reports that Nvidia has secured a major design win with its Vera CPUs with AI cloud provider Modal. According to Modal, preliminary evaluations showed that Vera could deliver twice the throughput of its existing AMD and Intel processors, although the company does not intend to cease using CPUs from its current suppliers.

Modal provides cloud infrastructure that enables AI developers to deploy AI agents that can perform complex operations autonomously over extended periods. Such workloads require substantial CPU resources for software execution, data processing, and other tasks that cannot be efficiently handled by GPUs. Modal currently relies exclusively on AMD and Intel processors for these operations, but its tests indicate that Nvidia's new Vera CPUs could significantly improve performance in its specific workloads. Of course, since Vera is based on an Arm instruction set architecture, Modal's decision to adopt Vera will require substantial modifications to its software. Nevertheless, Modal believes that the potential performance improvements justify the additional engineering effort.

The reported 2x throughput advantage is particularly interesting because agentic AI workloads can involve numerous independent tasks that compete for CPU cores, cache capacity, and memory bandwidth. However, Modal has not disclosed detailed benchmark configurations it used, specific AMD and Intel processor models, or performance-per-watt figures. Consequently, it remains unclear whether Vera's advantage is enabled by advantages of its Arm v9.2-based Olympus CPU cores that can decode and execute up to 10 instructions per cycle, its memory subsystem with 1.2 TB/s of bandwidth, or other architectural characteristics. Also note that tests compared Vera against currently available AMD and Intel processors rather than their upcoming generations that will compete against Vera in the coming years.

Latest Videos From Tom's Hardware Watch full video here:

Since Modal cannot port all of its software to Arm ISA overnight, the company will continue using x86 CPUs from AMD and Intel, according to Modal chief executive Erik Bernhardsson. Rather than sticking to one ISA for everything, Modal intends to operate a heterogeneous server fleet and select the most suitable processors for each workload. Naturally, the company intends to evaluate upcoming AMD and Intel processors once they become available to make its choices in the future.

For Nvidia, the agreement represents a major step toward making Vera a standalone server processor that commands a major share of the server market. The company expects Vera sales to generate at least $20 billion during its current fiscal year and estimates the potential total available market for these CPUs is approximately $200 billion. The company is on track to sell at least four million Vera CPUs in fiscal 2026.

The announcement comes shortly after Modal secured $750 million in financing led by Accel, which valued the company at $15.75 billion. Modal expects its annual revenue to reach $1 billion within the next year. The company's service consumption has increased 3X in the last 12 months, while revenue has surged more than 15 times compared with the previous year, Reuters reports.

Modal Had To Make Massive Changes To Move To NVIDIA's Vera CPUs As They Previously Relied on x86 Chips, But The Shift Granted Them A 2x Boost The NVIDIA Vera CPU continues to be changing the market perception of Arm-based CPUs for Agentic AI use cases. Arm itself has highlighted the advantages of its AGI CPUs over x86 options, but NVIDIA's option seems to be quickly becoming the choice for many firms that were previously running an x86 chip. Related Story Intel’s Jeff McVeigh Says Developers Shouldn’t Need Separate Software Paths For x86 CPUs, As AMD Folds Its ZenDNN Optimizations Into oneDNN Modal is one such firm that recently received its first Vera CPU servers at their San Francisco offices. The company has so far relied solely on x86 systems featuring AMD & Intel chips, so the move to an Arm-based ecosystem required changes to the infrastructure & image-built systems. Despite the painstaking changes, Modal terms the move to NVIDIA Vera as very impressive, delivering a 2x increase in AI throughput across Agentic AI sandboxes, and calling it an "incredibly compelling option". In most systems, throughput and latency are a tradeoff. Latency can be defined as the time that elapses from the start to the end of a task.

Throughput is the quantity of completed tasks per unit time. This tests the host system’s ability to concurrently interleave processes and make progress on them all simultaneously. The more densely you pack tasks, the higher the throughput. But once the CPU becomes fully utilized, individual task latency suffers due to contention. In terms of the Modal scheduler, it’s always tempting for us to run at a higher packing density, to squeeze more juice out of the host machines we have, and to offer a higher absolute scale that users can reach. But just as workloads are spiky within their containers, the absolute scale of the containers in our cluster is also spiky, which leaves us at the risk of overpacking host machines. To test NVIDIA Vera, Modal built a set of representative workloads and benchmarks for agentic sandboxes. This involves the development of "Agentless Agent Bench," which hosts a collection of 50 Terminal-Bench oracle solutions and verifiers. The benchmark shows both linear completion and concurrent throughput figures. The first tests showcased a nice improvement over x86 chips, but these were run without any load, essentially making them a pure straight-line latency test. Under load, NVIDIA's Vera CPU becomes a completely different beast. In throughput, Vera offered a 2x increase over an equivalent Intel Xeon "Granite Rapids" chip. This lead comes from the fact that unlike x86 CPUs, Vera doesn't slow down as jobs accumulate but rather rips through each one of them at its original pace. The results speak for themselves: Versus Intel Xeon: Up to 2x the task throughput per core.

Versus AMD EPYC: Over 6x the task throughput at 150 concurrent containers, with 124 logical CPUs enabled on each system. Vera’s killer feature is the ability to hold up under contention. Its high memory bandwidth allows for significantly more container workloads to pack per core, without CPU throttling - which explains why Vera pulls so far ahead of the alternatives in our benchmarks. At added CPU counts, the alternatives hit early throughput plateaus, while Vera continues to improve, suggesting we could push it even further than the node we had access to for benchmarking. Modal’s shift to NVIDIA’s Vera CPUs, despite the significant infrastructure and image-building changes needed to move from x86, delivered a clear 2× throughput boost in Agentic AI sandboxes. Under load, Vera maintains strong performance without the throttling typical of Intel and AMD CPUs, thanks to its high memory bandwidth and ability to pack more concurrent workloads per core. The result is a compelling Arm-based option that scales more effectively for dense, contention-heavy agentic workloads. proofCandidates.title: Modal Plans NVIDIA Vera Rollout for Sandboxes in First Arm Move
proofCandidates.summary: Modal announced plans to roll out NVIDIA's Vera Arm-based CPUs for its Sandboxes, its first departure from an all-x86 fleet. Benchmarks showed up to double the task throughput of an equivalent x86 machine under load. The company will work with NVIDIA and cloud providers to scale the Vera fleet.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Modal said in a company blog post on October 19, 2026 that it plans to roll out support for NVIDIA’s Arm-based Vera CPU to power Modal Sandboxes, the company’s first departure from an all-x86 fleet, after benchmark results it published showed up to double the task throughput of an equivalent x86 machine under load. NVIDIA hand-delivered Modal’s first Vera CPU server to the company’s San Francisco office in the week before the announcement, Modal said. Vera is NVIDIA’s Arm-compatible processor, built for the Vera Rubin GPU platform but also available as a standalone CPU server. Bringing Arm into the fleet would require changes across Modal’s infrastructure and image build system, which the company described as a huge change after a long history of running exclusively x86 machines. Multi-Tenant Noise and Burst Capacity Orchestrating a Sandbox product means running hundreds of concurrent containers and virtual machines on each cloud host, and Modal said the resulting multi-tenant clusters are noisy. Resource usage can be extremely spiky: a sandbox may sit mostly idle while waiting on a language model and then see CPU usage surge 10x above baseline because of an npm install or an expensive grep command. The shape of each workload is only known at runtime, so resource sizing is often a guess, and heterogeneous tenants packed into a single pool of compute create noisy-neighbor problems, where one customer’s behavior degrades another’s performance. Rather than require fixed reservations sized to maximum usage, Modal Sandboxes support bursting, which lets users reserve guaranteed capacity for their P50 usage and trust that padding inside the host node will absorb transient spikes. Modal said the approach has saved users millions of dollars, but acknowledged that it raises exposure to the noisy-neighbor effects that strict limits would otherwise avoid. Modal identified two prevalent Sandbox use cases: background agents, citing Ramp Inspect and agents running on Niteshift, and reinforcement-learning rollouts. Most training setups are still synchronous, the company said, so an entire fanout of CPU-bound rollouts must complete before idle GPUs can move to the next step, which means time saved on CPU is time saved on GPU. For background agents, the company said, faster execution means faster answers and lower CPU time, driving down the cost of goods sold. The Agentless Agent Bench To measure Vera, Modal built and released Agentless Agent Bench, a collection of 50 Terminal-Bench oracle solutions and verifiers with all network calls stripped out, prewarmed in concurrent Docker containers. Modal said building an agentic benchmark is difficult because most of the work done on its sandbox servers is not CPU-bound, so it assembled a concurrent and heterogeneous mix of the tasks agents and reinforcement-learning processes actually perform on the CPU, including compilation, file grepping, git operations and device emulation. According to the public repository, the benchmark is built on the terminal-bench-2.1 task dataset with Dockerfiles ported for Arm compatibility, and a run counts as completed only if the task verifier passes. In serial testing on an unloaded machine, which measures straight-line per-task latency, Modal found Vera was often faster than the other processors tested — Intel GNR, AMD Zen 5, and AWS Graviton 4 and 5 — but not always, and not by a particularly large margin, and the post’s author described being initially skeptical of the results. Under load, Modal reported, the results diverged. The throughput test increases the number of concurrent containers on the machine and loops as many verified task completions as possible in a fixed time. Modal said its early benchmarking runs showed up to double the task throughput on Vera compared with an equivalent x86 GNR machine, while individual task latency measured equal to or lower than on x86. In most systems, throughput and latency trade off as packing density rises until the CPU saturates, but Modal said Vera did not slow down as jobs accumulated and kept completing tasks at its original pace. Modal reported that Vera kept improving as logical CPU counts rose, while the other tested processors hit early throughput plateaus. The physical core boundaries of the tested machines were 128 for Intel GNR, 96 for Graviton and the GNR virtual machine, and 88 for Vera. Because the alternatives plateaued early, Modal said its results suggest it could push Vera even further than the single benchmark node it had access to. The company attributes Vera’s advantage under contention to its high memory bandwidth, which it said allows significantly more container workloads to pack onto each core without CPU throttling. For Modal’s scheduler, that means greater packing density and more forgiving burst protection; for Sandbox users, the company said, it means higher absolute scale and throughput without sacrificing latency. Vera’s Design and Production Status NVIDIA launched Vera on March 16, 2026 at its GTC conference, describing it as a processor purpose-built for agentic AI and reinforcement learning. The chip has 88 custom NVIDIA-designed Olympus cores, each able to run two tasks through a feature NVIDIA calls Spatial Multithreading, and a second-generation low-power memory subsystem built on LPDDR5X that delivers up to 1.2 TB/s of bandwidth. NVIDIA claims Vera delivers results with twice the efficiency and 50% faster than traditional CPUs. At the launch, NVIDIA also introduced a Vera CPU rack integrating 256 liquid-cooled CPUs, which it said can sustain more than 22,500 concurrent CPU environments, each running independently at full performance. NVIDIA said Vera is in full production, with partner availability in the second half of 2026, and named Alibaba Cloud, ByteDance, CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius, Nscale and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure among the cloud providers planning to deploy the CPU. Modal said it intends to work closely with NVIDIA and cloud providers to scale up its Vera fleet as the rollout proceeds.

proofCandidates.title: Modal Labs Sandboxes Hits $300M Run Rate: Isolated Code Execution Becomes Its Own Market
proofCandidates.summary: Modal Labs crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate and closed a $750 million Series D at a $15.75 billion valuation. Its Sandboxes product, an isolated code execution environment, now generates $300 million in annualized revenue, accounting for 30% of total ARR.
