proofCandidates.title: Fintech Increase Acquires Bank Charter, Eliminating BaaS Middleware That Broke Synapse
proofCandidates.summary: Increase acquired Twin City Bank of Longview, Washington, rebuilt it as Increase Bank, and became a federally regulated FDIC-member institution, collapsing the traditional three-layer BaaS structure into a single entity that simultaneously serves as technology provider and chartered bank. The charter eliminates the middleware ledger divergence risk responsible for the Synapse collapse that stranded approximately 100,000 consumers in 2024, replacing three separate ledgers with one authoritative system of record reconciling directly to the Federal Reserve in real time. Whether the charter's regulatory credibility and structural advantages outweigh the capital adequacy requirements, CRA obligations, and direct FDIC examination it imposes will determine if this model proves more durable than traditional BaaS under sustained regulatory pressure.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Fintech builders who route payments through Stripe, Ramp, or Gusto have been moving money through Increase's rails for years without knowing it. On Wednesday, the company behind that infrastructure did something the BaaS sector has talked about but rarely executed: it became the bank.

Increase launched Increase Bank — a federally regulated, FDIC-member institution — by acquiring and rebuilding Twin City Bank of Longview, Washington, into a purpose-built fintech infrastructure bank. The result collapses the three-layer structure that has defined banking-as-a-service for a decade, and that regulators have spent the past two years trying to police. There is no longer a sponsor bank on one side and a technology provider on the other. Increase is now both.

For fintech builders, that architectural change has a concrete implication: they can access payment rails, FDIC deposit accounts, and a real-time reconciling ledger through a single regulated entity — without stitching together a relationship with a sponsor bank and a separate API provider, and without the compliance handoffs between them that produced the Synapse disaster.

How BaaS Builds the Middle Layer That Keeps Breaking

The standard banking-as-a-service arrangement has always had a structural seam. A fintech facing the end customer, a middleware provider handling ledger management and API connectivity, and a chartered sponsor bank holding the regulated relationship — three entities, three ledgers, three sets of compliance obligations, and a cascade of third-party dependency that regulators have characterized as fundamentally difficult to supervise.

In July 2024, the Federal Reserve, FDIC, and OCC issued a joint statement flagging heightened risks in bank-fintech arrangements — risks that arise specifically when banks rely on partners to manage customer-facing activities. That statement came after a torrent of BaaS-related enforcement actions in early 2024, following which analysts at Klaros Group predicted that virtually every bank with a BaaS or embedded finance line of business would face some level of regulatory action. The core regulatory complaint was consistent: a fintech cannot outsource regulatory credibility to its sponsor bank, and the bank remains responsible for the customer-facing activity delivered through third parties — even when it cannot see or control what that third party's ledger says.

The specific mechanical failure that produced the Synapse bankruptcy illustrates why. When Synapse — the middleware provider at the center of dozens of fintech-bank arrangements — collapsed in 2024, neither the partner banks nor the fintech apps could resolve a ledger discrepancy that stranded an estimated 100,000 consumers and locked them out of their accounts. The discrepancy existed because Synapse maintained its own ledger, the partner banks maintained theirs, and the two did not agree. There was no authoritative single record.

What Increase Bank Does Differently at the Architecture Level

Increase has connected directly to the Federal Reserve since its founding in 2020 — not through an intermediary bank — which means its core has always been the system of record for account balances and transactions. That direct connection is what makes the bank charter a structural completion rather than a strategic pivot.

Increase Bank's technology maintains the system of record for account balances and transactions and reconciles to the Federal Reserve in real time. There is no middleware ledger that can diverge from the bank's records, because the bank and the technology are the same entity. A fintech client's account events are recorded once, in one ledger, held by one FDIC-member institution that also maintains direct connections to FedACH, Fedwire, Check 21, The Clearing House's Real-Time Payments network, FedNow, and Visa.

That architecture answers the specific failure mode the Synapse collapse made visible. The reconciliation gap that stranded 100,000 consumers was a ledger divergence problem — three entities maintaining separate records that could disagree. With Increase Bank, there is one entity and one record.

The combination also changes what a fintech client can do from day one. Karim Atiyeh, co-CEO of Ramp, described the operational difference in the bank's launch materials: "From the ability to open accounts synchronously, fully featured for every payment rail, from day one to the pace they ship new features, Increase just gets it." Synchronous account opening — an account that exists the moment an API call returns, rather than after a back-office process runs — is an architectural capability, not a product decision. It requires that the ledger and the charter be under the same roof.

Darragh Buckley's Methodical Path From Stripe to Bank Founder

The path from infrastructure provider to chartered bank ran through Twin City Bancorp, Inc., a small community bank holding company in Longview, Washington, about an hour north of Portland, Oregon. In April 2025, Buckley filed a change in bank control notice with the Federal Reserve Board, disclosing the acquisition of voting shares in Twin City Bancorp — a transaction that required FDIC approval before closing. The deal received FDIC non-objection for control and closed, and the renamed institution is now Increase Bank.

The acquisition was Buckley's third investment in a Washington community bank. That detail matters: Twin City Bank, with assets of approximately $75 million and a single branch, was a deliberately modest acquisition target — not a platform with an existing BaaS book of business to integrate, but a charter, an FDIC certificate, and a clean regulatory record with a Satisfactory Community Reinvestment Act rating.

Buckley's motivation traces directly to his time as Stripe's first employee, where he spent six years building and scaling Stripe's bank partner relationship with Wells Fargo and designing the programmatic controls for deposit account structures, money movement, regulation, cybersecurity, and privacy. The lesson he took from that work: when you are simultaneously solving business, technical, and risk problems, you need to drop down a layer. At Increase, dropping down a layer meant connecting directly to the Federal Reserve instead of relying on an intermediary bank to hold those connections. At Increase Bank, it means owning the intermediary entirely.

Increase became profitable in 2025, remains self-funded, and processed hundreds of billions of dollars annually across ACH, wires, RTP, FedNow, checks, and cards before the bank charter was added. Monthly payment volume tripled year over year. The company referred overflow business to competitors — including Grasshopper Bank and First Internet Bank of Indiana — rather than take on clients it could not serve well. That restraint is what makes the charter announcement legible as a natural evolution rather than an opportunistic pivot.

What the Charter Costs, and Why That Matters

Owning a bank charter is not a cost-free architectural upgrade. The same regulatory framework that gives Increase Bank its compliance credibility now imposes obligations that a pure-software BaaS provider does not face.

As an FDIC-member institution, Increase Bank is subject to regular safety-and-soundness examination, capital adequacy requirements, and full Community Reinvestment Act obligations — not just the contractual compliance commitments a fintech makes to a sponsor bank. Capital requirements constrain how quickly the bank can grow its balance sheet. CRA obligations require documented investment in the communities it serves. And regulatory examination means a federal agency now has direct access to the bank's records and operations, not just to its sponsor bank partner's records.

That tradeoff is the specific cost of eliminating the compliance handoff problem. A sponsored fintech can structure its relationship to minimize regulatory surface area. Increase Bank cannot. Whether that constraint produces a competitive disadvantage or a durable credibility advantage will depend on how the regulatory environment for BaaS alternatives evolves over the next several years. The sector that will watch that answer most closely is the one that just watched Synapse demonstrate what happens when the unregulated middle layer fails.

Diede van Lamoen, former Head of International at Stripe and an Increase advisor, framed the competitive stakes plainly: "A fintech company's ability to scale often comes down to whether they have a banking partner that can move at their pace, build solutions to the edge cases they are solving, and give them direct access to payment rails." The question the market will answer over the next two to three years is whether "banking partner" and "banking infrastructure" are more valuable when they are one entity subject to a single regulator — or whether the operational discipline the charter imposes makes Increase Bank slower to move than a lighter-weight BaaS competitor.

What Comes Next for a Sector Sorting Out Its Architecture

The fintech sector generated more than $650 billion in revenue in 2025 and grew at approximately 21% annually, according to McKinsey data cited in Increase's launch materials. That growth has happened almost entirely on top of the three-layer BaaS architecture the sector is now reassessing.

Increase is not the only fintech to pursue vertical integration through a bank acquisition. Column Financial Technologies, founded by William Hockey of Plaid, took the same approach with Northern California National Bank in 2021 and has built a national-charter-backed API banking infrastructure serving clients including Mercury and Brex. Lead Bank in Kansas City followed a similar trajectory under former Block executives. The common thread in each case is the same architectural insight Increase articulates: the compliance problem in BaaS is not a process problem that better contracts can fix — it is a structural problem that requires owning the regulated layer, not partnering with it.

What Increase Bank represents, in the context of an industry sorting out which BaaS models survive sustained regulatory pressure, is a data point: the charter-acquisition path is executable, and it is executable by a company that built its reputation specifically on engineering discipline and financial soundness rather than growth at speed.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between Increase Bank's model and standard banking-as-a-service?

Standard BaaS involves three separate entities: the fintech serving end customers, a middleware provider managing ledger and API connectivity, and a chartered sponsor bank holding the regulated relationship and deposit insurance. Each layer maintains its own records. When those records diverge — as they did in the Synapse bankruptcy — neither the bank nor the fintech has a clean path to resolution. Increase Bank collapses those three layers into one: Increase is the technology provider and the chartered FDIC-member bank simultaneously. Its core maintains a single system of record that reconciles directly to the Federal Reserve in real time, with no intermediate ledger that can diverge.

What happened with Synapse, and why does it matter here?

Synapse Financial Technologies was a BaaS middleware provider whose 2024 bankruptcy exposed a structural failure in the layered model: when Synapse's ledger diverged from its partner banks' records, approximately 100,000 end users were locked out of their accounts, with an estimated shortfall of $65 to $96 million. No single entity had an authoritative record of who was owed what. The Synapse failure demonstrated that the middleware layer in a BaaS arrangement carries a specific systemic risk — ledger divergence — that no amount of contractual language between the parties can fully resolve. Increase Bank's architecture eliminates the middleware layer, removing the divergence risk at its source.

Is owning a bank charter purely an advantage for a fintech company, or does it come with constraints?

Both. The charter gives Increase Bank regulatory credibility, direct payment rail access, and a single reconciling ledger — advantages that pure-software BaaS providers cannot match. But it also subjects Increase to capital adequacy requirements that constrain balance sheet growth, Community Reinvestment Act obligations that require investment in served communities, and direct regulatory examination by the FDIC. A partner-model BaaS provider can structure its operations to minimize regulatory surface area in ways a chartered bank cannot. Whether the credibility advantage outweighs the flexibility constraint is the competitive question the next several years of operating data will answer.

Who does Increase Bank currently serve, and what payments can it handle?

Increase's existing clients include Gusto, Ramp, and Stripe — companies that move money at scale across a range of payment types. Through Increase Bank's direct connections, it can process ACH transfers, wire transfers, Real-Time Payments via The Clearing House, FedNow transactions, check transfers under Check 21, and card issuance through Visa — all via a single API and a single chartered institution. The bank's FDIC membership and Federal Reserve connections were in place operationally before the charter conversion, meaning clients did not need to rebuild integrations when Increase Bank launched.

Increase also works with Grasshopper Bank, Indiana-based First Internet Bank and Core Bank, and those partnerships remain important, Buckley said. “We have many users who fundamentally need to be multi-bank, either for operational reasons or even their own corporate governance reasons,” he said. “A lot of times, the financial services that get provided through us are crucial to the business.” Clarification: This story’s headline has been updated to more clearly reflect that Buckley bought the bank.

proofCandidates.title: The Banking Infrastructure Founder Is Buying Community Banks - and That's the Point
proofCandidates.summary: Darragh Buckley, founder of Increase (a fintech processing over $100 billion annually by connecting directly to the Federal Reserve), has made a personal investment in Twin City Bank in Longview, Washington, acquiring a stake exceeding the 10% FDIC disclosure threshold—this being his third investment in a Washington community bank. Unlike typical fintech-bank partnerships where founders seek charters or regulatory control, Buckley frames this as an effort to understand banking infrastructure from the inside rather than building around it through APIs. The move positions Buckley's approach as distinct from the 2026 trend of fintechs and banks acquiring each other to own the opposite side of the relationship, with the article suggesting this strategy reflects a deeper bet on community banking's role in modernizing financial services.
proofCandidates.fullText: News/ Articles/ Articles Details The Banking Infrastructure Founder Is Buying Community Banks - and That's the Point Generated by AI Agent Arjun Varma Reviewed by The Newsroom Wednesday, Jul 29, 2026 9:19 am ET 3min read Aime Summary Overview The 5 Ws Opposite Sides Infobox - Darragh Buckley, founder of $100B/year fintech865201-- Increase, invested in Washington community bank Twin City, exceeding 10% FDIC threshold as personal stake. - Unlike typical fintech-bank partnerships, Buckley emphasizes understanding banking infrastructure from within, not through API layers or charter acquisitions. - His third Washington bank investment signals strategic focus on community banking's role in modernizing relationships while avoiding corporate control. - The move contrasts with 2026 fintech trends of charter chasing and bank acquisitions, highlighting infrastructure founders who prioritize operational depth over regulatory expansion. Darragh Buckley was employee number one at Stripe. He helped build the system that lets millions of companies accept payments online. Then he left and started Increase, a company that sits a layer below most fintech infrastructure: it connects directly to the Federal Reserve and exposes core banking functions through APIs. With fewer than 20 people, Increase now processes over $100 billion annually. And he just bought a significant stake in a small community bank in Longview, Washington. The headline version of this story would be about a fintech founder trying to own his rails. Buckley says that's not what's happening. The Twin City Bank stake - which exceeds the 10% threshold that requires FDIC disclosure - is a personal investment, not a corporate one. It's also his third investment in a Washington community bank. The FDIC approved it in 2026. The obvious question is why someone building next-generation banking infrastructure would invest in legacy institutions that exist in a town an hour north of Portland. The less obvious question, which is the more interesting one, is whether Buckley is doing something most fintech founders don't bother with: learning what the actual plumbing of banking looks like from the inside, rather than from the outside looking in. Most fintechs treat banks as black boxes. You build an API, you find a partner bank that will lend you its charter, you share revenue, and you hope the compliance layer doesn't blow up. That's the banking-as-a-service model. It works until it doesn't - and over the past two years, it hasn't. Regulatory scrutiny of BaaS partnerships has intensified. Compliance burdens have grown. Several high-profile BaaS relationships have collapsed, leaving fintechs scrambling. Increase was founded to avoid that problem at the architectural level. Instead of connecting to banks one by one - which is how most BaaS platforms work - Increase connects directly to the Federal Reserve and operates its own banking core. Its customers, including Ramp and Pipe, are other fintechs that need reliable money movement. But even if you've built a better layer, you still need to understand what happens at the bottom. The way to build software that improves an industry is not to read about it from the top. It's to look at the smallest instance of the problem and see what's actually broken. Buckley has said publicly that he envisions a future where community banks serve specific communities - dentists, families managing elderly parents' finances, local businesses that still need a relationship with someone who understands their cash flow. That's not a sexy vision. It doesn't read well in a pitch deck. But it's also not wrong. Community banks hold roughly a quarter of U.S. banking deposits, and they're the ones that will need to modernize or lose their customers to whoever figures out how to serve them digitally without killing the relationship model. The Twin City investment sends a signal, but not the one the competitor-funded PR campaign apparently tried to paint. This isn't about Increase trying to own a bank. Buckley's been clear about that. It's about a founder who understands that the people building the rails need to understand what's running on them. I suspect the real bet here is simpler than any of the narratives. Buckley probably thinks that if fintech infrastructure companies stay disconnected from the institutions they're trying to serve, they'll keep building the wrong things. The way to avoid that is not to buy the bank. It's to understand it well enough that you don't need to. This is part of a broader pattern in fintech right now. The first half of 2026 has seen two dozen fintech-related companies apply for or conditionally receive bank charters from the OCC. Circle Internet Group received its national trust bank charter in July. Morgan Stanley and Nomura's Laser Digital both got conditional approvals. On the flip side, banks are buying fintechs - Capital One announced plans to acquire Brex, Coastal Community Bank announced plans to acquire its BaaS partner GreenFi. Everyone is trying to own the other side of the relationship. Buckley is doing something different. He's not chasing a charter for Increase, and he's not trying to make Twin City Bank into an Increase project. He's putting his own money where the action is - in the small institutions that the fintech industry talks about serving but rarely visits. The limitation, of course, is that I don't know exactly how large his Twin City stake is - the disclosure only says it exceeds 10%. It could be 11%, it could be a controlling interest. The exact number changes the read. At the low end, it's a genuine community investment. At the high end, it's a quiet power play that Buckley isn't yet ready to describe publicly. Either way, the pattern of three Washington bank investments is a signal about where he thinks the future of banking infrastructure needs to connect. The test to watch is whether Increase's product decisions start reflecting a deeper understanding of community banking. If they do, Buckley bought insight. If they don't, he just bought a nice diversification. The product will tell. What this suggests for anyone evaluating fintech infrastructure companies: the founders who understand the institutions they're serving - not just the APIs they're building - tend to build things that last. The ones who don't, tend to get acquired by the banks they were supposed to replace. The question for Buckley's investors isn't whether Increase needs a bank charter. It's whether Increase can stay small, stay focused on the plumbing nobody else wants to touch, and process $100 billion with fewer than 20 people while the bigger companies spend hundreds of millions chasing charters they can't figure out how to use. That's a different kind of leverage, and it's harder to see coming. proofCandidates.title: Introducing Increase Bank, Built on the Infrastructure Powering Hundreds of Billions in Money Movement
proofCandidates.summary: Increase Bank launched as an FDIC-member institution, providing regulated banking services and modern banking infrastructure APIs to fintech companies. The bank, founded by former Stripe operator Darragh Buckley, enables companies to move, store, and lend money with direct connections to the Federal Reserve, The Clearing House, and Visa. The platform serves existing clients including Gusto, Ramp, and Stripe, which collectively move hundreds of billions of dollars through Increase's infrastructure.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Increase Bank gives fintechs a regulated banking partner purpose-built for how modern companies operate: programmable, direct, and built to scale

Announcing the launch of Increase Bank, bringing a modern bank core together with regulated banking services to help teams build the best financial products with greater speed, precision, and control. Founded in 2020, Increase’s banking infrastructure and APIs enable companies like Gusto, Ramp, and Stripe to move, store, and lend hundreds of billions of dollars. With the addition of Increase Bank, an FDIC-member institution, fintech companies now have access to a bank engineered for their needs. Read More on Fintech : Global FinTech Interview: AI and the future of fintech with Hugh Cumming, CTO, Vena “This is a bank built by a team of product-obsessed operators for ambitious companies that are just as obsessed with building the best possible products for their customers,” said Darragh Buckley, founder of Increase. “This is a bank built by a team of product-obsessed operators for ambitious companies that are just as obsessed with building the best possible products for their customers,” said Darragh Buckley, founder of Increase. “It is programmable at scale and designed for reliability, speed, and flexibility.” The idea for Increase was born out of Buckley’s experience building Stripe from its earliest days, where he saw the need for banking infrastructure built with the same engineering depth as the fintechs relying on it. Since that time, the fintech industry has become one of the fastest-growing sectors in technology, generating over $650 billion in revenue in 2025 and growing at about 21 percent year over year. Increase now includes Increase Bank and a modern banking core with direct connections to the Federal Reserve, The Clearing House, and Visa. Increase’s technology maintains the system of record for account balances and transactions and reconciles to the Federal Reserve in real time. This gives fintechs full control over accounts and enables them to operate with their bank at the same speed and scale at which they operate their business. “A fintech company’s ability to scale often comes down to whether they have a banking partner that can move at their pace, build solutions to the edge cases they are solving, and give them direct access to payment rails,” said Diede van Lamoen, former Head of International at Stripe and advisor. “Increase was built by people who have first-hand experience with these challenges and a drive to support users from the first payment to their billionth.” Increase’s technology is trusted by some of the largest fintechs and software platforms in the United States, providing flexible, transparent, and reliable primitives for money movement, storage, and card issuance. “At Ramp, we are building AI for finance, and we must move fast to save our customers’ most valuable resources – time and money. Increase provides the banking infrastructure we need to do just that. From the ability to open accounts synchronously, fully featured for every payment rail, from day one to the pace they ship new features, Increase just gets it,” said Karim Atiyeh, Ramp’s Co-CEO. Catch more Fintech Insights : Global FinTech Innovations Are Transforming Banking into Continuous Financial Guidance [To share your insights with us, please write to psen@itechseries.com ]

proofCandidates.title: Zip adds Column N.A. as second US banking partner | The Paypers
proofCandidates.summary: Zip Co. announced that Column N.A., a nationally chartered bank, will act as a bank partner for its unsecured US instalment lending products. The agreement is Zip's second banking partnership, intended to support funding cost efficiencies and operational resilience. Neither company disclosed financial terms or lending volume.
proofCandidates.fullText:
ASX-listed Zip Co, which provides digital financial services to consumers in the US, announced on that Column N.A., a nationally chartered bank, will act as a bank partner for its unsecured US instalment lending products. The agreement is Zip’s second banking partnership in the market and extends the bank partnership model through which the company offers credit products to US consumers.
Column N.A. operates under a US national bank charter and is federally regulated. Its addition brings a nationally chartered bank into Zip’s US partner base, which the company presents as part of a wider effort to diversify its banking relationships.
According to Zip, the expanded model is intended to support funding cost efficiencies and strengthen operational resilience. The company ties the move directly to the scale its US business has reached. At the same time, the initiative frames a broader partner structure as a requirement for an operation of its current size rather than an incremental adjustment.
Funding diversification as a growth lever
Rory Herriman, President and Interim CEO at Zip US, said that maintaining a diversified funding platform is central to the company’s ability to serve customers as it continues to grow. The official described the partnership as reinforcing the foundations of the business ahead of its next phase of growth. Furthermore, it is also intended to support the continued expansion of access to what the company describes as transparent and responsible credit for millions of US consumers.
According to Brian Fishbein, Chief Investment Officer at Column N.A., the agreement adds a consumer lender of Zip’s reach to a platform that already supports a range of consumer lending products for financial services firms. The representative indicated that Column expects to support Zip through its technology, particularly as Zip moves into new products and serves new customers.
What the partnership signals
Neither company disclosed financial terms, the lending volume expected to run through the new partnership, or a timeline for any new product launches. Zip also did not name its existing bank partner in the announcement.
The arrangement nonetheless points to two priorities for Zip in the US: reducing dependence on a single banking relationship, and preparing its funding structure for product expansion. Adding a federally regulated, nationally chartered bank also gives the company an additional regulated counterparty for its unsecured lending activity.
For Column N.A., the partnership reflects its focus on providing bank and technology infrastructure to consumer lending businesses operating at scale. The extent to which the new partnership supports Zip’s planned product expansion is likely to become clearer once those products are introduced.

proofCandidates.fullText:
Solana gets the default spot for stablecoins at FDIC-insured bank

Market Musing-g

Column, an FDIC-member U.S. bank, has launched stablecoin support built directly into its banking core, allowing customers to send, receive and convert stablecoins like USDC and USDT into and out of U.S. dollars instantly, around the clock.

Solana , a high-speed blockchain network designed for fast and low-cost transactions, is the default network for stablecoin activity on the platform, with support for Ethereum and other major chains also available.

Related: Billionaire says Bitcoin is 'worthless' after CLARITY Act failure

A stablecoin is a cryptocurrency designed to hold a steady value, typically by being backed one-to-one by a traditional currency like the U.S. dollar.

Stablecoins are widely used for payments, trading and moving money across borders, but until now have relied on third-party intermediaries to bridge the gap between the blockchain and the traditional banking system.

Solana as the default rail

Column chose Solana as its default chain for stablecoin transactions. Amelia Daly, head of partnerships at the Solana Foundation, said the integration marks a shift from theory to production.

"Column made them native to a bank with Solana as the default network, and moved the frontier of financial services from theory into production," Daly told TheStreet Roundtable.

The choice reflects Solana's growing position in stablecoin infrastructure.

Trending on TheStreet Roundtable:

The network processed over $4.7 trillion in stablecoin volume over the past year, and stablecoin circulating supply on Solana reached approximately $14.7 billion in August 2026, nearly triple the level from a year earlier, according to Blockworks data

One ledger, no middlemen

Column's approach eliminates the gap between blockchain and banking. Because stablecoins are built directly into its own infrastructure, a customer's stablecoin address and bank account sit on the same ledger.

Conversions between stablecoins and dollars happen instantly with no prefunding required, the company said

A customer can receive USDC at 9 p.m. on a Saturday and pay it out over the RTP instant payment network to any U.S. bank account within seconds. The product is already scaling, with tens of billions in annualized volume, Column said.

TLDR KEYPOINTS Column is broadening its stablecoin card issuing services to compete directly with Mastercard and Marqeta.

The expansion targets the payments infrastructure layer, where stablecoin-linked cards are an emerging product category.

Regulatory clarity and issuer adoption will be key factors in determining how quickly Column can gain ground.

Column Aims to Challenge Card Issuing Incumbents

Competing with Mastercard and Marqeta on issuing infrastructure is a significant technical and regulatory undertaking. Neither incumbent is exiting the space; both have existing crypto card partnerships in market. Column would need to offer meaningful differentiation, whether on cost, compliance tooling, or settlement speed, to convert issuers already on established platforms.

What to Watch as Stablecoin Card Infrastructure Develops

Regulatory treatment of stablecoin card programs remains a live variable. Proposed U.S. crypto legislation such as the CLARITY Act could reshape how stablecoin issuers and card programs are licensed, directly affecting the competitive dynamics Column is entering.

Interest rate policy also matters for stablecoin yield economics. As the Federal Reserve's rate trajectory shifts, the yield spread available to stablecoin card issuers on reserve assets will affect product economics for all players in this market.

The key watchpoints: whether Column secures card network sponsorship, which regulated stablecoin issuers it partners with, and how quickly it can demonstrate compliant end-to-end issuance at scale. The outcome will depend entirely on the details and execution of Column's expanded offerings, none of which have been publicly specified.

Summary Column launched four products covering stablecoins, card issuing, global banking and multicurrency accounts.

USDC and USDT can be converted into U.S. dollars and connected with domestic and international payment rails around the clock.

Column built its own issuer processor and now provides banking, processing and capital through one integration.

Verified customers globally can access U.S. dollar or local currency accounts and cards using Column’s infrastructure.

William Hockey said the new products are already moving billions of dollars for major fintech companies.

According to Column co founder William Hockey, the rollout completes a years long effort to build the underlying components needed for technology companies to create financial products without connecting separate banks, payment orchestrators and processing providers. Hockey announced the products on Sept. 16, saying each service is already processing billions of dollars for fintech companies including Ramp, Brex, Bilt, Mercury, Slash and Kapital.

Column said the new stablecoin infrastructure makes USDC and USDT interoperable with U.S. dollars and the payment networks connected to its banking platform. Transfers and conversions can operate around the clock, while clients can move funds between stablecoins, bank accounts and domestic or international payment rails without relying on an intermediary provider.

The launch comes as stablecoins increasingly move into payment and banking infrastructure. crypto.news previously reported that stablecoin card spending surpassed $10.9 billion cumulatively, based on Paymentscan data cited by RedotPay in August. Monthly spending crossed $1 billion for the first time in July, compared with approximately $339.4 million a year earlier.

Column stablecoin infrastructure connects crypto and bank payments

Column’s stablecoin product allows businesses to receive and send USDC and USDT while moving between digital dollars and traditional bank money. Hockey said the functionality was built directly into Column and operates without middlemen.

One example provided by the company involves receiving USDC from Mongolia, immediately converting the funds into U.S. dollars and splitting the payment. Part of the money could then be sent to a U.S. community bank through FedNow while another portion is converted into euros and sent through SWIFT.

Hockey described the process as possible through a few API calls and said it could be completed within seconds.

Column’s product arrives as fintech companies build similar connections between stablecoins and traditional payment systems. Ramp, which Column named among the companies using its infrastructure, launched stablecoin accounts on Solana in July. Ramp said businesses could hold USDC and USDT and make payments to vendors in more than 140 countries, with settlement available in more than 40 local currencies.

Local currency conversion remains a separate part of the payment process even when the underlying stablecoin transfer settles quickly. Gravity Team CEO Mārtiņš Beņķītis said in August that stablecoin transfers still depend on local liquidity, banking connections and payout infrastructure when recipients need spendable domestic currency.

Column is combining those functions inside its banking stack by connecting stablecoins with its existing dollar accounts and payment rails.

A second product gives customers access to Column’s full card issuing stack, including the bank, processing infrastructure and capital through one integration.

Column has sponsored card programs for several years but has now built its own issuer processor from the ground up, according to Hockey. Clients can use the infrastructure to create debit, credit and stablecoin backed cards across the Mastercard and Visa networks.

Bringing the processor in house means Column can provide the banking relationship and card processing layer rather than requiring a fintech company to combine separate providers for those functions.

Stablecoin cards have become a growing part of the card market. Visa said earlier this month that more than 160 programs linked to stablecoins were operating globally during its fiscal second quarter of 2026. Payment volume from the programs rose nearly 200% year over year, while Visa’s stablecoin settlement volume surpassed a $20 billion annualized rate.

Mastercard has been expanding its settlement infrastructure in parallel. In June, the company added six regulated stablecoins to its settlement network, including USDC, PYUSD, USDG, USDP, RLUSD and SoFiUSD. Mastercard said the system could settle transactions outside traditional banking hours, including weekends and holidays.

Column’s card platform supports both Visa and Mastercard while allowing stablecoin balances to sit within the same infrastructure used for conventional card programs.

Global banking opens Column accounts beyond the U.S.

Column’s third product extends its account and card infrastructure to verified customers outside the United States.

Businesses using the service can issue U.S. dollar or local currency accounts and cards to eligible customers globally. Column said companies can use the same infrastructure and compliance tools that support their domestic operations instead of creating a separate technology stack for international users.

The company did not provide a complete list of supported jurisdictions in the announcement. Availability therefore depends on the markets covered by Column’s global banking infrastructure and its customer verification requirements.

For businesses operating across multiple countries, the global banking service can be combined with Column’s stablecoin and card products. A customer could hold funds through an account, receive a stablecoin payment and use the balance through a card without moving between separately integrated providers, based on the product flow described by Hockey.

Column said the products were designed to work with one another because they share the company’s underlying financial infrastructure.

Multicurrency accounts connect to international payment systems

Column’s fourth product adds individually numbered accounts for foreign currencies, allowing customers to receive, hold and send money in currencies other than the U.S. dollar.

Funds can be converted instantly between supported foreign currencies and dollars, according to the company. The accounts connect with international payment networks, including SEPA Instant, giving clients another route for local and cross border payouts.

Hockey provided another example in his announcement in which a company receives USDC, converts the stablecoin into dollars and divides the balance between different payment destinations. One portion could travel over FedNow, another could be converted into euros and sent through SWIFT, while a third could be directed back to a card.

Column said the workflow could be completed within seconds because its stablecoin, banking, card and foreign currency products use the same underlying financial components.

The company has positioned the four products as an alternative to fintech stacks assembled from separate banks, issuer processors, payment orchestrators and other vendors. Hockey said businesses can instead use Column as the single bank behind the financial products they build.

Column did not disclose individual transaction volumes for the four services, but Hockey said every product announced this week is already moving billions of dollars at scale for some of the world’s largest fintech companies.

proofCandidates.title: Column Just Ate the Card Processor: A Self-Funded Bank Shows Where Stablecoin Spend Margin Concentrates
proofCandidates.summary: Column, a self-funded national bank, launched stablecoin transactions and full-stack card issuing, consolidating bank, processor, and capital roles. It reported $153 million in 2025 revenue, up 219% year over year, with $83 million from interest income and $70 million from interchange. The move signals where stablecoin card margins concentrate, with networks like Visa and Mastercard as the investable exposure.
proofCandidates.fullText: The card in your wallet is never really one thing. Pull it apart and you find a bank that holds the account and the network license, a processor that authorizes and settles transactions, and often a separate lender that fronts the credit or capital. For the fintech companies that build those cards, the default was to stitch all three together from independent vendors and hand each one a slice of the economics — a sponsor bank here, a processor there, a capital provider somewhere else. Last week a company you've never heard of announced it was sinking the seams. Column — a nationally chartered bank that acts as software infrastructure for other fintechs and says it moved more than $4.5 trillion last year — launched stablecoin transactions, full-stack card issuing, global banking, and multicurrency accounts in a single release. Its founder, Plaid co-founder William Hockey, called it "completing the stack". The point is that a fintech card program no longer needs a bank, a processor, and a capital partner at all; Column says it is now all three, in one FDIC-member entity that owns its own card numbers. The structural move matters beyond one private company, because Column is the infrastructure-company equivalent of a tell: it shows where the margin in the fastest-growing payment category is concentrating, and who is positioned to capture it. Why owning the charter changes the arithmetic Start with what Column actually is, because the difference from its competitors is the whole story. Column N.A. is not a processor renting a bank's license. It is a national bank, member FDIC, founded in 2021 when the founders put roughly $50 million of their own money into buying Northern California National Bank and rebuilt it as an API-first platform. A directory of the nineteen major card-issuing platforms in the U.S. sorts the field by three things: license structure, network access, and who actually holds the bank identification number, the BIN. On all three, Column sits in the top category — the group of "global infrastructure" providers that hold their own licenses and BINs, alongside Cross River, Green DotGDOT--, and Pathward — rather than the processors (Lithic, Marqeta, Galileo) or orchestrators (Unit, Synctera) that depend on someone else's sponsorship and split the fees accordingly. That ownership is the economic engine. In the old banking-as-a-service model, a card program's revenue is carved up between the middleware platform, the sponsor bank, and the capital provider. Column breaks that fragmentation by being all of them: it takes deposits, so it earns the interest; it issues and processes cards, so it keeps the interchange and usage fees; and it offers its own lending balance sheet, so the credit economics stay inside too. Sacra estimates Column's revenue reached about $153 million in 2025, up 219% year over year, with roughly $83 million from interest income on deposits and $70 million from interchange and usage-based charges. The math is the strategy: the less you have to share, the more of every dollar of client activity is yours. The stablecoin card is the part to watch Column's card launch on its own would be a consolidation story. Its stablecoin piece is what turns it into a growth story, because that is where the volume is exploding. Stablecoin-linked cards are the bridge that turns crypto holdings into ordinary merchant spending. Instead of the merchant accepting crypto, the card converts a USDC or USDT balance into dollars at the point of sale on the Visa and Mastercard rails, settling outside banking hours. Retail spending through these cards has roughly doubled in the past year; card-based stablecoin volume grew about 106% year over year, reaching an annualized rate of roughly $18 billion by early 2026. It is still a rounding error against global card spend — under 1% — but it is growing like a breakout category, and a national bank that holds the whole stack, settled in USDC against the dollar across U.S. and international rails, is positioned to keep that margin rather than hand it to a processor. There is a genuine moat in regulatory form here. A pure stablecoin processor can build the rails, but it cannot custody the dollars or hold the deposit base the way a chartered bank can. Column's pitch is that its clients get stablecoin interoperability and card acceptance without abandoning the safety and regulatory envelope of an insured bank. For a retail investor, the honest reading is that the stablecoin card rail is real and compounding, and the companies that will capture it are the ones that own a charter, the network access, and a balance sheet at once — not the middleware that rents them. What should give a retail investor pause The case for the category is not a case for Column as a position, because you cannot buy it. The company is entirely founder- and employee-owned, with no venture investors and no public shares. So the useful questions are what it signals and which investable exposures capture the same tailwind. The first caution is concentration. Column's revenue is tied to a small set of marquee clients — Mercury, Brex, Ramp, Bilt, Slash, plus lending partners like Propel and Best Egg. That has been the growth engine, but it means the whole business leans on a handful of fintechs that could churn, consolidate, or blow up. The second is that nearly half its 2025 revenue was interest income on deposits, a number that rises and falls with the rate cycle rather than with product adoption. For a shareholder-oriented takeaway, the cleanest public counterparty to the stablecoin card boom is not Column — it is the networks themselves. Every one of these cards, Column's included, runs on Visa or Mastercard and pays them a fee on each transaction, and the still-tiny share of card spend these stablecoin products represent is the headroom. A self-funded bank deciding it needs to own the processor it used to route through is a signal about where payments margin is going; the investor who wants that exposure without taking on a private bank's math may find the network that collects tolls on every card to be the sturdier bet. Column's launch is a reminder that the payment stack you thought was fixed is being rebuilt from the inside, and that in the stablecoin era the people who win own the whole thing — the charter, the rails, and the balance sheet. The rest are hoping to be paid to stand in the middle.

-- MUNDI, the FinTech company powering export growth for Mexican firms and their supply chain, announced the completion of a new financing facility for up to $150 million from Column, a nationally chartered bank that provides regulated financial infrastructure for technology companies; marking Column's first financing partnership with a trade-finance-focused FinTech in Mexico. The facility strengthens MUNDIʼs funding capacity as it continues to scale its trade finance offering for companies across Mexico, and comes at a moment when Mexican businesspeople face uncertainty around the terms of cross-border trade under the ongoing USMCA review. The new facility adds to MUNDIʼs existing credit lines and together with other recent debt facility renewals, giving MUNDI the capacity to grow its receivables portfolio to up to $325 million, more than double its previous capacity.

Mexican exporters have historically faced limited access to dollar-denominated financing, despite the country's growing role in North American trade: U.S. imports from Mexico reached $534.3 billion in 2025, with momentum continuing into 2026. Micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) are the backbone of Mexico's economy, yet they produce less than 7% of the country's exports, in part because formal financing remains underused: supplier financing is the most common source for Mexican companies, while financing from foreign-domiciled banks remains marginal.

When financing does reach Mexican companies, the impact is significant: 7x more investment, 6x more revenue, 5x more production, and 4x more employment. This is the gap MUNDI was built to close, partnering with Column to accelerate growth in Mexico-U.S. trade finance by providing working capital solutions tailored to the realities of cross-border commerce.

"This partnership isn't just about more capital, it's about a fundamentally faster and more flexible way to fund Mexican exporters and their supply chain," said Martin Pustilnick, co-Founder and CEO of MUNDI. "Column's platform lets us draw funding daily, in minutes. At a time when the rules of trade between Mexico and the U.S. are being renegotiated, having the capital and the speed to back our clients isn't a nice-to-have, it's essential. This partnership more than doubles our capacity to grow and gives us room to bring new products to market."

“Cross-border trade is essential to the North American economy, and weʼre proud to put Columnʼs powerful banking infrastructure to work connecting exporters with dollar funding,ˮ said Brian Fishbein, Chief Investment Officer at Column. “MUNDI is a champion of Mexican trade. Todayʼs partnership will scale their capacity to quickly deploy reliable capital to Mexican exporters and supply chains, and build economic dynamism across North America.ˮ

Access to fast, flexible, dollar-denominated financing is becoming a decisive factor for Mexican exporters' ability to compete and grow, particularly as the terms of North American trade are being renegotiated under the USMCA review. For exporters and their supply chains, working capital constraints can mean the difference between capturing new international demand and losing it to better-financed competitors.

MUNDI is positioned to keep expanding access to that capital for a growing base of Mexican exporters and their supply chain with this new facility, while also using its added capacity to develop new products in the months ahead.

About Column:

Column N.A. , Member FDIC, is a nationally chartered bank that provides regulated financial infrastructure for technology companies. Founded in 2019 by Plaid co-founder William Hockey, Column serves as the banking backbone for modern financial products and powers the world's most sophisticated fintechs, such as Brex, Bilt, Wise, Mercury, and more. With a custom-built banking core, ledger, data model, and a direct connection to the Federal Reserve, Column eliminates the inefficiencies of legacy banks and middleware — creating a faster and more reliable banking platform. Beyond payments and accounts, Column enables national lending and credit products, powering API-based loan-origination partnerships and deploying its balance sheet to fund lenders through debt financing and loan purchases.

About MUNDI:

MUNDI is a fintech company supporting Mexican companies to scale their businesses through financing services specialized in international trade, serving all types of exporters and their supply chain. Over its six years of operation, MUNDI has partnered with nearly 600 companies to facilitate transactions from Mexico to more than 50 countries, totaling over $2.5 billion.

MUNDI is backed by world-class investors and partners, including USV, Haymaker Ventures, FJ Labs, GMO, Upper90, and Base10, as well as J.P. Morgan and SVB (a division of First Citizens), in addition to Allianz and Coface.

proofCandidates.title: Rent fintech Flex applies for ILC charter
proofCandidates.summary: Rent fintech Flex has applied with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. and Utah Department of Financial Institutions for an industrial loan company charter to become an industrial bank, the company announced Friday. The bank would be based in the Salt Lake City area and issue Flex's core credit products, including its flexible payment solution Flex Rent, directly to customers, eliminating the need for current sponsor banks Lead Bank and Column Bank. Flex has processed more than $40 billion in rent since 2019 for over 3.2 million users and is part of a broader trend of companies—including Klarna, Stellantis, Ford, and GM—seeking ILC charters under the current regulatory environment.
proofCandidates.fullText: Rent fintech Flex has applied with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. and Utah Department of Financial Institutions to become an industrial bank, the company announced Friday. “A bank charter allows us to build directly on a foundation of federal deposit insurance and full state and federal bank regulatory oversight, strengthening the products millions of renters already rely on,” Shragie Lichtenstein, CEO and co-founder of Flex, said in a statement. “Rent is the single biggest bill in most people’s lives, and it’s often the one least adapted to how they’re actually paid. This charter gives us a permanent, regulated foundation to keep closing that gap.” Jeff Berkson – who until May served as chief risk officer at WebBank, according to LinkedIn – will be Flex Bank’s proposed CEO. The bank will be based in the Salt Lake City area and operate nationally through digital channels. The bank would issue Flex’s core credit products, including the flexible payment solution Flex Rent, directly to customers. Flex has processed more than $40 billion in rent since 2019 for more than 3.2 million users, and has helped them avoid more than $780 million in late fees, the company said, adding that it does not compound interest or permit the stacking of loans. Trump-era regulators have seen a sharp increase in new charter applications. FDIC Chair Travis Hill last year touted the industrial loan company charter as one of a handful of ways to boost the establishment of new banks. Buy now, pay later juggernaut Klarna applied this month for an ILC charter. Car maker Stellantis received approval in May to launch an ILC and other automotive stalwarts, including Ford and GM, got green lights in January. Investment firm Edward Jones followed in February. Some lawmakers, with backing from the banking industry, have argued that an ILC charter exempts companies from the definition of a “bank” under the Bank Holding Company Act. As long as ILCs don’t offer demand deposit accounts, they can bypass oversight by the Federal Reserve, the politicians contend. In January, Sens. John Kennedy, R-LA, and Andy Kim, D-NJ, introduced a bill to close what they called the “shadow banking loophole.” The bill is now sitting with the Senate Banking Committee. Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Banking Dive free daily newsletter The trade group Independent Community Bankers of America said in May that cutting the Fed out of ILC supervision “leav[es] a dangerous gap in safety and soundness oversight and introducing unnecessary systemic risk into the banking system.” Last year, Kim and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-MA, proposed a moratorium on commercially owned ILC charters until such entities are defined as “banks” under the BHC Act. The ILC isn’t the only charter that has seen refreshed interest since President Donald Trump reentered the White House. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency has seen an uptick in applications for national trust charters, popular among cryptocurrency firms. A handful of fintechs – including Upstart, Mercury and Valt Bank – have opted to try for full bank charters. Flex currently uses Lead Bank and Column Bank as its sponsor banks. An ILC charter for Flex would make those partnerships unnecessary.

proofCandidates.fullText:
core offering: Column is a nationally chartered bank that provides API-first programmable banking infrastructure for software companies and fintech platforms. Through a REST API, partners can create FDIC-insured bank accounts, issue cards, initiate ACH/wire/real-time/international payments, and originate, finance, or sell loans. The platform connects directly to the Federal Reserve, The Clearing House (RTP), FedNow, SWIFT, and card networks, and is licensed as Column N.A. to operate nationwide with over 800 partner banks in its FDIC sweep network.
differentiator: Column is the only nationally chartered bank designed specifically for developers and software companies. Unlike traditional banks that use middleware and sponsor bank relationships, Column runs its own dedicated hardware connected directly to the Federal Reserve, TCH, and SWIFT. This 'close to the metal' approach provides granular control and eliminates vendor dependencies. The company is 100% founder and employee owned with no external investors, enabling focus on long-term customer value rather than growth metrics.
functional benefit: Real-time payment processing via RTP and FedNow networks; FDIC-insured deposits through 800+ partner bank sweep network; API-accessible bank accounts, cards, lending, and payment rails; 99.999% uptime guarantee; $4.5T+ annual transaction volume capacity; No. 1 position in US real-time payments
problem solved: Column solves the fundamental problem that fintech companies and software platforms face when trying to build financial products: the complexity and cost of partnering with traditional banks, dealing with multiple middleware providers, and navigating fragmented payment infrastructure. By providing a unified API-accessible banking platform with direct connections to payment networks, Column enables partners to embed banking, payments, and lending into their products without becoming a bank themselves.
quantifiable outcome: 99.999% uptime - highest of any bank
quantifiable outcome: Moving $4.5T+ annual transaction volume
quantifiable outcome: No. 1 issuer of real-time payments in the US
quantifiable outcome: Over $100B international payments processed annually
product overview: Column is a nationally chartered bank built as API-first banking infrastructure for software companies, offering a unified platform with modular products across payments and lending. The platform operates through two main categories: Infrastructure products (ACH, Wire, Book Transfers, Ledger, Bank Accounts, Card Programs, Checks, Realtime Payments, and International Wires) that enable companies to move, hold, and lend dollars at scale; and Lending products (Loan Origination, Debt Financing, and Loan Purchase) that help companies offer and scale credit programs. All products are accessible via a REST API with direct connections to Federal Reserve, The Clearing House, SWIFT, and card networks (Visa, Mastercard). The company processes over $4.5 trillion in annual transaction volume with 99.999% uptime and serves as the banking backbone for fintech companies including Brex, Mercury, Ramp, and Best Egg.

proofCandidates.title: Stripe is giving off early Google vibes—for good and for bad
proofCandidates.summary: Stripe has acquired crypto firms Privy and Bridge, verification firm Ourum, billing firm Metronome, and AI distribution service OpenRouter for about $7.5 billion. The company's PayPal acquisition fell through after a share-price uptick made its offer look too cheap. Analysts see the moves as strategic but note antitrust risks ahead.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Newsletters Term Sheet Stripe is giving off early Google vibes—for good and for bad By Jeff John Roberts Jeff John Roberts Editor, Finance and Crypto Down Arrow Button Icon By Jeff John Roberts Jeff John Roberts Editor, Finance and Crypto Down Arrow Button Icon September 2, 2026, 8:12 AM ET The Stripe cofounders: CEO Patrick Collison (left) with president John Collison. David Paul Morris—Getty Images Add Fortune on Google for similar content. Add us on Google Add us on Google Good morning, it’s finance editor Jeff John Roberts pinch-hitting for Allie. Term Sheet readers of a certain age may recall when a young and still up-and-coming company called Google went on an acquisition spree for the ages. In a four-year span starting in 2003, the search giant hoovered up two ad tech firms, DoubleClick and AdSense, that gave it a full suite of digital advertising tools. And for good measure, it acquired the firm that built the tech behind Google Earth as well as two little startups called Android and YouTube. That shrewd run of M&A is a big reason why Google, now Alphabet, is today one of the dominant companies on the planet. Recommended Video I raise all of this because Stripe has been on a shopping spree of its own that, if things go right, could one day prove as successful as what Google pulled off 20 years before. Leaving aside its aborted play for PayPal (more on that in a moment), Stripe has since late 2024 acquired two crypto players, Privy and Bridge, that were leaders in the fields of wallets and stablecoins respectively. The fintech giant has also purchased a firm called Ourum that specializes in account verification and bank transfers, as well as Metronome, which handles usage-based billing. For good measure, Stripe this month closed on a deal worth around $7.5 billion for the buzzy AI distribution service OpenRouter. Put it all together and Stripe, like Google before it, is strategically absorbing firms that will help it consolidate its existing lead in its core service, while also building capacity in two fields—in this case blockchain and AI—that will define the next decade of technology. That brings us to the aborted PayPal deal. The would-be acquisition, which was cooked up this spring, came undone this week after a recent uptick in PayPal’s share price suddenly made Stripe’s original offer of $60.50 per share look too cheap. Had the deal worked out, it would have added a critical additional piece to Stripe’s growing empire: A massive consumer-facing business to complement its existing merchant-heavy customer base. According to James Wester, a research director at Javelin Strategies, the PayPal deal falling through may have been for the best. Wester points out that it would have been a tough cultural fit for Stripe, which he says is defined by a developer-focused ethos, and has little in common with a lumbering older brand like PayPal. Wester also notes that Stripe can only bite off so much since, as a private company, it is relatively constrained in how much capital it has to throw around. Google, by contrast, carried out two of its major acquisitions—DoubleClick and YouTube—when it was flush with cash from its 2004 IPO. As for the quality of Stripe’s acquisitions, and any forthcoming ones, it’s hard to predict how they will pan out. Looking back at Google’s purchase of its ad tech stack, the obvious reaction is “OMG, what a steal, how did regulators let that go ahead?”—but that’s with the benefit of hindsight. It remains to be seen whether Stripe’s purchases will prove as prescient. As one competitor to whom I made the Google comparison pointed out, Yahoo made a lot of acquisitions in that era too—only to flame out and get bought by the phone company a decade later. Wester, though, thinks it’s unlikely that will be Stripe’s fate. “As much as the analyst in me wants to look at these latest acquisitions for AI and stablecoins with a jaundiced eye, I can’t help but think they’ve been pretty good at this so far,” he said, adding that Stripe has been a master of anticipating where the payments landscape is going next. In addition to a penchant for M&A, Stripe has another attribute that invites comparison to early era Google: Its knack for public relations. Even as the company has grown into a behemoth, its charismatic founders have preserved a down-home Irish image, burnished by the company’s “Cheeky Pint” video interview series. And unlike most fast-growing companies, Stripe makes no unforced errors. This can’t go on forever, of course. Just as sheer size and media glare forced Google to drop its “Don’t Be Evil” corporate logo, Stripe is likely to show sharper elbows in coming years. Then, there is the matter of antitrust, which became one of the few forces to slow Google down. Stripe is still not of the scale to worry about that yet—and antitrust seems to be out the window in the Trump era in any case—but don’t be surprised if all those acquisitions cause legal trouble down the road. For now, though, Stripe can enjoy its current sweet spot of being powerful and likable at the same time, just as Google did long ago. See you tomorrow, Jeff John Roberts

proofCandidates.title: US Payment Service Providers: How Stripe at $1.4T and the Rejected $30B Settlement Reshaped 2024
proofCandidates.summary: In March 2025, Stripe disclosed $1.4 trillion in 2024 total payment volume, up 38% year-on-year, joining Adyen and Block as trillion-dollar-scale US payment service providers in a market where merchant payment choices have expanded significantly. On June 25, 2024, US District Judge Margo Brodie formally rejected the proposed $30 billion Visa-Mastercard antitrust settlement, calling projected merchant savings 'paltry' relative to annual fees and sending the parties back to negotiate on interchange and surcharge terms. The article analyzes how PSP economics are being reshaped through 2024-2025 by embedded finance, vertical software platforms (Toast, Square/Block, Shopify), and payment operations layers, with card acceptance margins compressing while alternative revenue streams emerge.
proofCandidates.fullText:
Share Share Share Share Email In March 2025 Stripe disclosed $1.4 trillion in 2024 total payment volume, up 38 per cent year on year, in its annual update. Stripe is no longer the only firm in the US payment-service-provider category operating at trillion-dollar scale: Adyen and Block each report large 2024 numbers, and the legacy acquirers (Fiserv, Worldpay, Global Payments) process meaningful volume across more traditional merchant relationships. A US merchant accepting cards in 2026 has more choices for who processes the payment than for who supplies the espresso machine in the same store. What they get, on top of acceptance, varies sharply. What a US Payment Service Provider Actually Does A payment service provider sits between a merchant and the card networks. The PSP onboards the merchant, runs underwriting and ongoing risk checks, runs the gateway that captures the customer’s card details, routes the authorisation request to the issuing bank, and remits net settlement back to the merchant’s deposit account. Some PSPs also act as the merchant acquirer, holding the regulatory relationship with the card networks directly. Others, often called payment facilitators or independent sales organisations, sit on top of a sponsor bank and wholesale that relationship to many merchants underneath them. The economic stack is layered. Interchange goes to the issuing bank, network fees go to Visa or Mastercard, and what remains is split between the acquirer and any PSPs or value-added resellers in the stack. The US merchant pays a blended rate, but the components have different competitive dynamics. Interchange is regulated for debit but not credit. Network fees are set by the schemes. The acquirer and PSP margins are the genuinely competitive piece, and they have been compressing for years. The Rejected $30 Billion Settlement The largest single regulatory event for US PSPs in the 2024–2025 period was the rejection of the proposed Visa-Mastercard $30 billion antitrust settlement. The proposed deal would have reduced US credit-card interchange and given merchants more flexibility on surcharging, in exchange for releasing the card networks from the long-running US merchant antitrust litigation. On June 25, 2024 US District Judge Margo Brodie formally rejected the proposed settlement, calling the projected merchant savings “paltry” relative to the estimated annual fees merchants pay the networks. CNN’s contemporaneous coverage documents the ruling and the judge’s reasoning. The rejection sent the parties back to the table and re-opened the surcharge and interchange conversation for US retailers. Who Is Capturing the Margin Four broad groups captured most of the new US payments-tech margin in 2024 and 2025. The first is the scaled platforms: Stripe, Adyen, Block, and similar firms that combine acceptance, value-added services, and developer-led distribution. The second is the issuer-processor stack: Marqeta, Lithic, and Galileo continue to power most US neobanks and embedded card programmes. The third is the vertical software stack: Toast for restaurants, Mindbody for fitness, ServiceTitan for trades, Procore for construction, Shopify and similar e-commerce platforms across retail. These firms bundle payments with software, which lets them subsidise the acceptance fee from software revenue. The fourth is the payment-operations layer: Modern Treasury, Increase, Orum, and similar API platforms that let companies move money across multiple rails through a single integration. Margin trends differ across the four groups. Card acceptance margins compressed through 2024 and 2025 as competition intensified and as the regulatory backdrop continued to push toward lower interchange. Payment operations margins held, since the API layer charges per transaction rather than per percentage. The vertical software platforms are absorbing some of the margin compression at the acceptance layer by reframing payments as a feature of their broader operating system rather than as a standalone product. Embedded Finance and the Vertical Software Wedge Embedded finance reshaped US PSP economics through 2024 and 2025. The wedge starts with payment acceptance and expands into instant payouts, business credit, FDIC-insured deposit accounts, payroll, and increasingly insurance. Toast Capital cash advances on top of Toast payment processing is the textbook example, with eligibility driven by the merchant’s payment history through the platform. Square does the same for the small-business customers on its product. The lifetime-value math for a vertical software platform now starts with payments and expands from there, which is the opposite of a traditional PSP whose payments-only customer has limited upside. The implications cascade. Traditional PSPs lose merchants to vertical platforms. Vertical platforms route their payment volume through infrastructure-layer payment facilitators (Finix, Rainforest, Tilled, Stripe Connect). Infrastructure payfacs commoditise the underlying acquiring relationship. The acquiring banks move further upstream, handling the regulated piece while the application layer moves downstream into software. None of this is finished, but the direction was clear by the second half of 2025. Date Event Headline number March 2024 Visa and Mastercard reach proposed $30 billion antitrust settlement with US merchants $30B proposed June 25, 2024 US District Judge Margo Brodie formally rejects the proposed settlement Rejected February 27, 2025 Stripe reports $1.4 trillion in 2024 total payment volume, up 38 per cent year on year $1.4T TPV Sources: CNN coverage of the settlement rejection and Stripe 2024 update. What to Watch Through 2027 Three threads will shape US payment service providers through 2027. First, the next chapter of the merchant antitrust litigation will determine whether a successor settlement, or a renewed court fight, reshapes US credit-card interchange. The original $30 billion proposal failed because the court found the relief inadequate; subsequent proposals will have to clear that bar. Second, the steady consolidation among small and mid-tier PSPs continues, with several private equity firms running roll-up strategies across the legacy independent-sales-organisation portfolio. Third, the CFPB has signalled supervisory interest in how payfac-as-a-service vendors handle merchant onboarding compliance, and any new guidance through 2026 will shape the cost of operating the payfac model. The interesting US PSP question for 2026 is not which provider has the lowest rate. It is whose model can absorb the next round of margin compression and still fund the software and risk investment required to stay in front of a US merchant base that has more options, and falling switching costs, than ever before. The PSPs that figure that out first will capture the next decade. The ones that do not will become the contracting back office of someone else’s growth story. proofCandidates.title: BitPay Adds Bill Payment to Its Crypto Wallet – Digital Transactions
proofCandidates.summary: BitPay added bill payment to its cryptocurrency wallet, partnering with Method Financial to let users pay bills at over 5,000 billers. The feature supports various cryptocurrencies and is available in 20 U.S. states. BitPay CEO Stephen Pair called it a game-changing solution for crypto users and the unbanked.
proofCandidates.fullText:
BitPay Adds Bill Payment to Its Crypto Wallet

BitPay Inc. expanded the payment capabilities of its cryptocurrency wallet Tuesday with inclusion of bill payment. BitPay users can now pay bills with digital currency at more than 5,000 billers, the Atlanta-based company says. To enable bill payment, BitPay has partnered with Method Financial, an Austin, Texas-based provider of embedded banking services. Method Financial is serving as the bill-payment aggregator. To enable bill payment through its wallet, BitPay is using customer-provided information to search for any bill available for payment, such as monthly bills reported to credit bureaus and used to help determine a consumer’s credit score. Examples of such bills include credit card statements, mortgages, and car loans. To pay bills, BitPay users verify their identity using BitPay ID. Next, they tap the Connect Bills tab. After clicking on the tab, Method Financial searches for and presents available bills. Users then select the bills they want to pay. The more than 5,000 billers available to BitPay users are part of Method Financial’s network of more than 10,000 merchants. “Having launched the first crypto-powered debit card years ago for our users, we wanted to expand our offerings to enable app users to buy, swap, spend, and now pay bills,” Bill Zielke, BitPay’s chief revenue and chief marketing officer, tells Digital Transactions News by email. “Bill Pay is a natural … extension of our product set aimed at users who transact and live life using crypto.” BitPay supports paying bills with cryptocurrencies such ERC-20 tokens and stablecoins, Bitcoin, Ethereum, Bitcoin Cash, Dogecoin, and Litecoin. Other cryptocurrencies supported by the BitPay wallet include Shiba Inu, ApeCoin, Polygon, Dai, USD Coin, Binance USD, Wrapped Bitcoin, Pax Dollar, Gemini Dollar, and Euro Coin. BitPay Bill Pay is available in Alabama, Alaska, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, Ohio, Oregon, South Dakota, Tennessee, and Washington state. “Paying everyday bills without a bank account is a monumental step for the crypto and unbanked community,” says BitPay chief executive Stephen Pair, in a statement. “BitPay customers are some of the most prominent crypto spenders in the world, so we believe this will be a game-changing solution for both crypto users and service providers.”
